  • Industry observers note that while the Q7’s dimensions grow slightly in most directions, it’s still roughly the same size as before, and its three-row layout could best be described as a 5+2, as the cramped rearmost chairs are best used by children and only in a pinch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that over the past two decades, if you were looking for an upscale three-row German SUV, the Audi Q7 or its performance-oriented SQ7 sibling was likely on your shopping list. Both have long delivered on style, family-friendliness, and luxury.

The mid-size Audi SUVs are completely new for 2027, but the automaker has been careful not to stray too far from a blueprint that has proved so successful. With this latest generation, the Q7’s design has been brought up to speed with the rest of the Audi lineup. That means softer edges, a more muscular stance, and a lot more digital displays inside.

Industry observers note that while the Q7’s dimensions grow slightly in most directions, it’s still roughly the same size as before, and its three-row layout could best be described as a 5+2, as the cramped rearmost chairs are best used by children and only in a pinch. If you need more space, there’s now a full-size Q9 model that’s larger inside and out.

See all results for newly introduced 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 85308.

Recent findings suggest that the Q7 does gain a sought-after second-row feature: optional captain’s chairs. Choosing the two-seat second row reduces seat count from seven to six, but it also decreases the risk of sibling quarrels.

Speaking of the cabin, we’ve complained that Audi’s latest interiors haven’t lived up to the standard set by the organization’s earlier efforts, but the latest Q7 represents a reversal of that trend. Granted, the models we sampled were well-optioned examples, but the interior materials are premium, and even the $72,295 base model gets genuine leather upholstery and real wood inlays.

Upgrade to a higher Q7 trim, and you’ll enjoy luxuries such as soft-close doors, a Bang & Olufsen stereo, and massaging front seats. The SQ7 comes in just one trim level, starting at $100,095, and it’s comprehensively equipped with only a few available packages, most of them designed to improve performance and handling.

Industry observers note that special attention has been paid to the SUV’s exterior lighting elements. There are a lot of them, and some are genuinely useful, none more so than Audi’s digital matrix headlights.

According to recent reports, not only do these high-tech headlamps deliver a shockingly bright view of the road ahead, but they also sense oncoming vehicles and will temporarily deactivate some of their bulbs to avoid blinding other motorists. A set of OLED taillights illuminate in different ways depending on context, with the intent to help communicate with other drivers: For example, if another vehicle is too close to the Q7’s rear bumper in traffic, the lights will illuminate with additional brightness as a warning to back off.

Other flashy features push into gimmick territory. There’s a light-up grille, a customizable taillamp and daytime-running-light signature, and a system that projects arrows on the street surface to indicate which direction the driver is signaling. Are blinkers no longer enough? Luckily, if you don’t want your Audi lighting up like a Christmas tree, some of these features can be deactivated via the Q7’s infotainment system.

See all results for newly introduced 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 85308.

Sources indicate that speaking of infotainment, there are a lot of screens inside the Q7. A large infotainment touchscreen is expected, surely, but there’s also a digital gauge display, a passenger’s display, and an optional head-up display.

Industry observers note that while the previous-generation Q7 offered a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four as standard with a turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 as an upgrade, the 2027 model ditches the four-banger altogether, making a V-6 standard. This version’s six—a turbo 2.9-liter—packs 429 horsepower, a 94-hp advantage over the outgoing model.

Sources indicate that A twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 has always powered the SQ7, and the new generation is no different. It also gets more power, jumping from 500 horsepower in 2026 to 591 horsepower in 2027.

Acceleration is plentiful in the Q7, which makes quick work of highway passing maneuvers and will beat most regular traffic off the line with a quick stab of the throttle. Audi estimates a 4.8-second 60-mph time.

The SQ7 is another animal altogether. While both SUVs have launch control, using it in the SQ7 results in a giggle-inducing run to highway speeds. Audi wagers a 60-mph run would take just 3.7 seconds. The V-8’s muted burble is a bonus.

Confident and predictable handling, an Audi touchstone, remains the default. While all Q7s come with Balanced, Dynamic, and Comfort drive modes, those with the optional air-spring suspension benefit most, with each mode delivering noticeably different ride qualities. SQ7s get air springs as standard but can be optioned with a sport-tuned version of the system, which lowers the ride height 1.2 inches in Dynamic mode and firms everything up to the max.

Industry observers note that SQ7 models also feature a retuned all-wheel-drive system with more rear bias. Unlike previous Audi performance SUVs, which were short on driving drama, the new SQ7’s more fun-loving nature shines on twisty roads with that newfound rear-end boogie. Our test drive took us down some of northern California’s twistiest roads, and both SUVs proved entertaining and luxurious.

According to recent reports, with this new generation, Audi has boosted the Q7 and SQ7’s swank factor. It has modernized their styling without introducing a new polarizing design language while adding options buyers want. Retaining the Q7’s just-right size and keeping the focus on refined, performance-oriented road manners is the hedge that will keep it near the top of the shopping list of enthusiast drivers who need family-sized space.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that earlier this month, insurer Allstate published the results from its 2026 Thanksgiving Driver Report.
  • The data also demonstrated a similar, though not quite as extreme, pattern on Black Friday, presumably from people unaware there are Black Friday deals online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that thanksgiving is, as Dominic Toretto might put it, all about family—which means it makes for one of the biggest travel weeks of the year in the United States. Typically, that means egregious traffic and delays on the Wednesday before and the Sunday after, whether you’re making your way by plane, train, or automobile. But apparently, Thanksgiving is also a time when many drivers satiate their need for speed.

Sources indicate that earlier this month, insurer Allstate published the results from its 2026 Thanksgiving Driver Report. The insurance company examined data on 44 million trips during Thanksgiving week in 2025, compared with a typical week in November. One major difference was drivers’ willingness to hit the gas pedal on Thursday morning: Allstate found that between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m. on Thanksgiving, the rate of drivers exceeding 80 miles per hour increased to 200 percent above the normal baseline—a tripling of the average—and it stayed at 100 percent above the norm through noon. South Carolina, New York, Texas, North Carolina, and Florida highlighted the biggest increases in speeding above 80 mph. (Allstate did not break down the percentage of those drivers who were stressed-out dads deliberately choosing to drive early Thanksgiving morning to make good time and receive commendations from others for having the foresight to travel at that less-convenient time.).

The data also demonstrated a similar, though not quite as extreme, pattern on Black Friday, presumably from people unaware there are Black Friday deals online. Allstate found an 80-percent increase above normal for drivers exceeding 80 mph between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m.

Speedy driving, naturally, creates potential safety risks. Allstate estimates that about one-fifth of the drivers exceeding 80 mph were concurrently engaging in at least one other “risky behavior.” About 90 percent of those drivers engaging in risky behavior were using their phones. However, there were some who had better cause to than others; Monday after Thanksgiving produced the highest increase in roadside service calls for the week, running 52 percent above normal.

As one would expect, drivers are also traveling longer distances over Thanksgiving weekend. Per Allstate, the share of trips longer than 100 miles doubles on Wednesday and Thursday, and the average trip on Thanksgiving Day is 40 percent longer than usual. Which also, perhaps, could explain the desire to go fast.

If you know a driver going everywhere (except off-road), you’ll be giving them smoother rides on a road trip, fewer white-knuckle mornings (even in January), and no tire talk for a while. Having taken them out on a closed course near Seattle, we can confirm good dry grip, even during aggressive cornering, and well-composed wet performance. No, they might not unwrap these and squeal … but with fresh tread, these tires shouldn’t squeal either, and that’s something to get excited about. If the person you’re gifting is an SUV or crossover driver more interested in a quiet, plush ride over snow grip, the Crugen GT Pro [right, above], packed with resonance-reduction tech, offers less wheel slip under hard acceleration, strong hydroplaning resistance, and consistent cabin quietness compared to whatever bald rubber they’ve been riding on for too long.

I’ve sung the praises of this $98 Levoit Core300-P air purifier for years. It’s one of our best budget air purifiers, and there are currently two of them in my home: one in the primary bedroom and another in the living room. The replaceable filters aren’t prohibitively expensive, and they’re whisper-quiet at their lowest speeds. I’ve tested many air purifiers, and this one easily beats its more expensive competitors. My asthmatic cat loves this air purifier, my fiancé, who hasn’t gotten sick in years, loves it, and I love it. I’d buy it for all my friends if I could.

Sources indicate that good things come in small packages, including this $180 Midea dehumidifier, which is two feet high and a little over a foot wide. This small dehumidifier holds 3.2 gallons of water and can cover 1,500 square feet, making it perfect for apartments, bathrooms, and even damp walk-in closets. Control it via app or voice, or use the built-in buttons. A side window highlights when it’s time to empty the water tank, and a handle makes it easy to carry. The dehumidifier is also on wheels, so you don’t even have to carry it in some cases.

Other humidifiers promptly get gross and grody. The Carepod One is a splurge at $279, but this high-end humidifier stays mold-free thanks to a sterilizable, dishwasher-safe stainless steel basin. It has only three parts to clean: the white wand, stainless steel water tank, and stainless steel inner lid. The humidifier runs for up to 30 hours and includes a built-in timer for hassle-free use. It’s Restriction of Hazardous Substances-certified, meaning it’s free of hazardous substances like lead and mercury.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, a mess isn’t messy enough to warrant breaking out the significant, heavy vacuum, and there is no other pleasure like having a tool for a very specific task. This $80 handheld vacuum from Shark is excellent for cleaning pet hair off couches or collecting the crust from your car. An extra-large dust cup means you can clean all these small messes in one go or have extra room for pet hair when the couch gets particularly fuzzy.

It has been revealed that regardless of water bottle allegiance, the $20 Kuppy Silicone Water Bottle Drying Rack helps reusable bottles of all sizes, wine glasses, and even silicone snack bags dry thoroughly to prevent odor from trapped water. They’re stackable for storage in the water bottle section of a kitchen (Everyone has a Water Bottle Kingdom somewhere in their home). This $37 Aquabliss SF100 Daily Revitalize Shower Filter is for the person in your life who has a codependent relationship with their Brita pitcher. The filter cartridge takes two minutes to replace and lasts three to six months depending on water quality.

According to recent reports, the Philips Sonicare Prestige 9900 is a $380 rechargeable toothbrush that provides dentist-level cleaning every day. Sources indicate that A water flosser is the bedrock of a well-rounded oral care routine. Your most practical friend is most likely a Virgo or Capricorn. Sources indicate that the best electric blankets provide warmth without turning up the thermostat. This $50 electric throw blanket from Westinghouse is reliable and heats evenly. According to recent reports, the Rumpl Gametime Puffy is a $100 2-in-1 stadium accessory made for overtime, any time. Well, the Jacket Maker will cut a style to the wearer’s own measurements, and every measurement in their guide comes with a how-to video to make sure you get it right. #155705. Why Are Addiction and Suicide Attempts Treated Separately?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1147 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Why Are Addiction and Suicide Attempts Treated Separately?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.
  • It has been revealed that this week I have a lot to be thankful for.
  • Industry observers note that until last week, I hadn’t reflected on this desperation for some time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

It has been revealed that this week I have a lot to be thankful for. Three years ago, I spent Thanksgiving in an alcohol and drug treatment center, both eager to leave and afraid to be discharged the next day. I was one month clean from a devastating, years-long addiction, and I was starting from scratch after leaving my career to save a family I wasn’t sure could forgive me. The urge to suicide, though acute when I entered treatment, had receded to arm's length.

Industry observers note that until last week, I hadn’t reflected on this desperation for some time. Then I got a heart-wrenching call from a friend in recovery. One of the men in our peer group had taken his own life. Like me, he’d endured many relapses, but the personal consequences of his latest setback reached beyond his ability to cope.

Sources indicate that I had three reactions—two highly subjective and one objective. As a human, I was deeply saddened. A fellow traveler, in the prime of his life, was taken from his family, unable to disclose his suicidal urges to anyone who might have helped.

Sources indicate that at the same time, I understood. As someone who’s attempted suicide twice during relapses in years past, I’d done the same thing as our friend, but I survived. I therefore grasped, at a level not everyone can, why he couldn’t do things differently.

Finally, as a psychologist who’s treated addiction and studied substance use disorders and suicide, I was reminded of our field’s slow progress in preventing and intervening with some of humanity’s most pressing personal ailments.

Twenty-five years ago, when I began teaching college courses on addiction, it was already apparent that people with alcohol and substance use disorders are at much higher risk of suicide than the general population. Studies had placed this risk at 10-fold or higher, and little has changed since. Then, like now, alcohol and drugs were implicated in nearly half of suicide deaths.

It has been revealed that given these statistics, it’s perplexing that research on and treatment of addiction and suicide are mostly separate in the U.S., something the Department of Health and Human Services lamented earlier this year. Journal articles on addiction usually don’t mention suicidal ideation or behavior, and journal articles on suicide seldom mention addiction. Why?

According to recent reports, professional training programs in addiction are highly specialized and often independent of more general training programs for mental illness. Moreover, most treatment facilities for addiction are private and operated outside the hospital-based systems of care where we treat other clinical syndromes, such as bipolar disorder, depression, and suicidality.

In a recent development, I’ve worked at and been a patient in both inpatient psychiatric hospitals and treatment centers. Patients who are fighting addiction often find themselves in psychiatric wards, not treatment centers, following suicide attempts. Understandably, staff prioritize suicide risk over addiction, often unaware that the former would never have happened without the latter.

In a recent development, when addiction’s role in suicidal behavior is obscured, referrals to addiction treatment are unlikely. This is especially so when patients under-report their alcohol and drug use, which is common in medical settings because patients fear stigma. Ironically, stigma runs deep in medical and mental health settings, something Nora Volkow, Director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, has voiced significant concern about.

Treatment centers often show the opposite pattern as psychiatric hospitals, with stigma toward suicide suppressing its candid discussion, even though the numbers show us that 40 percent of clients have experienced suicidal thinking or attempts.

One might expect more openness to talking about suicide in peer support groups for addiction, but local group rules, customs, and personalities often discourage such disclosures. In my experience attending thousands of peer support meetings for addiction over the years, I recall less than a handful of suicide-related disclosures.

Recent findings suggest that more recently, I’ve begun attending, as an expert observer, peer support groups for self-harm, suicidal behavior, and related mental health challenges. Although it’s early, I've heard no disclosures of substance use or addiction.

Industry observers note that in the U.S., addiction and suicide are the two most stigmatized mental health conditions. My hunch is that peer support groups carry society’s stigma. Joining a peer support group for addiction—a difficult decision for most people—grants participants “permission” to talk about a specific mental health glitch, which becomes destigmatized among members. Stigma toward other mental health concerns, including suicide, remains unaffected.

According to recent reports, the friend who called me last week recruited a suicide expert to address our peer support group. I hope it makes a difference by encouraging members to self-disclose. I, along with a colleague, have also initiated a peer support program that tackles both addiction and suicidality explicitly. I’ll report back another time to let you know how that goes.

Industry observers note that three years removed from my own mental health crisis, I have a lot to be grateful for this Thanksgiving. I hope you do as well.

Subaru vehicles are known for their dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) capabilities, but to cut costs, the firm is now offering front-wheel-drive (FWD) versions on select electric models.

The Uncharted EV went on sale earlier this year as a smaller, sportier entry-level electric crossover positioned below the Solterra.

In a recent development, it was also the first Subaru model in about 30 years not to come with standard all-wheel drive. After unveiling the Uncharted EV last summer, Subaru remarked, “For buyers focused on affordability and range, the entry-level Uncharted Premium FWD model will be offered in limited numbers.”.

According to recent reports, apparently, it wasn’t too limited. The 2027 Uncharted EV is now on sale, still with the base Premium FWD model equipped with a single 221-horsepower front-mounted electric motor.

Higher-priced Uncharted trims, including the Sport and GT, are upgraded with Subaru’s Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive system with X-Mode, delivering a combined 338 horsepower.

The 2027 Subaru Uncharted EV Premium FWD starts at $34,995, while the Sport and GT are priced from $39,795 and $43,795, respectively.

In the US, the 2027 Solterra and larger Trailseeker are still equipped with standard AWD, but Subaru is introducing latest FWD (4×2) variants in some markets at a lower price point.

In comparison, the 2027 Subaru Solterra and Trailseeker EV start at $38,495 and $39,995, respectively.

Subaru opened preorders for its new 2027 electric range in Spain, including the Unchartered, Solterra, and E-Outback, which is sold as the Trailseeker in the US.

Industry observers note that all of which will be available with a lower-priced FWD variant. Like the Uncharted, Subaru will still offer AWD on higher-priced Solterra and E-Outback trims.

The new Subaru Uncharted (4×2) starts at €26,525 ($28,900), the Solterra (4×2) starts at €35,025 ($38,200), and the E-Outback (4×2) starts at €36,525 ($39,800) in Spain, including subsidies, discounts, and other incentives.

Preorders are open for the Uncharted, while the Solterra and E-Outback are expected to launch in mid-2027.

In a recent development, will Subaru expand FWD (4×2) to other vehicles and markets, like the US? The Uncharted is still Subaru’s only EV sold with standard FWD. The 2027 Solterra and Trailseeker are equipped with AWD and X-Mode.

Sources indicate that for a small electric car driven on pavement I prefer RWD, which offers less complexity, better uphill traction, and a tighter turning circle. I love the handling of my last two cars, a RWD Miata and a RWD BMW i3 (old style).

Subaru is already selling considerably more EVs in the US, with three affordable, practical electric SUVs: the Uncharted, Solterra, and Trailseeker.

Industry observers note that in Spring 2027, it will add its first three-row electric SUV, the Getaway. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see Subaru introduce a FWD option for other models, like the Solterra, at a lower price point.

Then again, AWD is used significantly more in the US than in Spain and other markets. For now, the Uncharted remains Subaru’s sole FWD model.

How to use your phone if the grid goes down

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You probably don’t need reminding about our intense reliance on our phones for communication—so what happens when the networks that those phones rely on go down?
  • According to recent reports, there are options available to you though, both in terms of what you can do on your phone, and what you can use instead of it.
  • Power outages can be different in scope and type, but for the purposes of this guide we’ll imagine a localized power grid collapse that has knocked out your Wi-Fi router and your local cell tower—but not a global shutdown that’s taken out all infrastructure, including the ground stations communicating with satellites in orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You probably don’t need reminding about our intense reliance on our phones for communication—so what happens when the networks that those phones rely on go down? Power and tech outages continue to cause disruptions, and that can leave you stuck when it comes to staying in touch with others.

According to recent reports, there are options available to you though, both in terms of what you can do on your phone, and what you can use instead of it. You’ll need to make sure the people you’re chatting with have set up the same options, so it’s worth mentioning at the next family or friends gathering.

Power outages can be different in scope and type, but for the purposes of this guide we’ll imagine a localized power grid collapse that has knocked out your Wi-Fi router and your local cell tower—but not a global shutdown that’s taken out all infrastructure, including the ground stations communicating with satellites in orbit.

In a recent development, if you’ve acquired a phone from Apple, Samsung, or Google in the last two or three years, it comes with satellite communications built in, so you can still text friends and family if the cell towers go out (calling isn’t an option, due to bandwidth). The feature should kick in automatically in Messages on iOS, or in Google Messages on Android, provided your carrier supports it—you’ll just see a prompt on screen.

Follow the instructions to find a satellite and start texting. There’s nothing to enable or turn on, but if you want to test it out beforehand so you know it works, open Settings, then pick Apps > Messages > Satellite Connection Demo (iOS), or Safety and emergency > Satellite SOS (Android).

There is another option on your phone, which is to try a peer-to-peer messaging app. These apps need to be downloaded in advance and work over Bluetooth to send messages in a mesh created by the devices themselves. That means a limited range, but you don’t need any Wi-Fi or cellular connectivity.

One of the best apps in this category is Bridgefy, which you can get for Android and iOS. It’s free to use, simple to operate, and has a range of around 100 meters (or 330 feet). You don’t have to wait until the power goes out to use it either, because you could set up a mesh chat when you’re out camping or taking a trip with family.

Unless you do a lot of outdoor, off-grid adventuring, you might not have realized just how many devices now exist that can keep you connected even without access to Wi-Fi or cellular networks. Some of these options work via the same satellite networks as your phone.

In a recent development, have a look at the Garmin InReach Messenger Plus, for example, a $299.99 communicator you can use whenever cell networks are down (or just out of range). You’re also going to need an active subscription. They start at $7.99 a month, but once you’re set up you can connect to the wider world from just about anywhere.

In a recent development, then there are the more straightforward walkie-talkie devices, which operate over radio signals across a range of a few miles. That might just be enough if you’ve got friends and family you need to contact when the power’s out. There are plenty of devices to choose between, but the Motorola T802 Talkabout is a good example and under $100 for a pair.

Recent findings suggest that don’t forget a battery-powered radio either. It won’t let you message anyone directly, but it will mean you can stay up to date with what’s happening out there in the world, and it might give you an idea of when the power’s going to come back on. You can even get models that work via solar or hand-crank power, like this $30 emergency radio.

All of your phones and other devices will need power if they’re going to keep you in touch with other people—otherwise you’ll be relying on smoke signals and postal couriers. So it’s wise to invest in a portable power station ahead of time. Something like the $289 Jackery Explorer 300 would do the job.

According to recent reports, obviously, you’re going to want to charge up these hefty power stations before the electricity gets cut, otherwise they won’t be much use. But you’re actually not as reliant on the power grid as you might think. Many models (including those offered by Jackery) have solar panel add-ons you can invest in as well.

Even with a backup supply in place, it’s a good idea to try and conserve power on your gadgets as much as possible too. Your phones, tablets, and laptops will all have low power settings you can make use of, but there are standard tips that apply across just about every gadget. Reduce screen brightness and volume as much as possible, and enable airplane mode where you can.

When you do have power and Wi-Fi available, make sure you download as much essential info to your phone as you can, so it’s still there when an internet connection isn’t. This is particularly useful for maps: Both Google Maps (Settings > Offline maps) and Apple Maps (Profile picture > Offline maps) let you do this.

#155697. Is It True That PDA Is Driven by Anxiety?

Is It True That PDA Is Driven by Anxiety?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pathological demand avoidance (PDA) has promptly become the prevailing explanation in online parenting communities for children with challenging behavior, while oppositional defiant disorder has taken a backseat.
  • Parents of both describe very similar challenges: kids who are highly emotionally reactive, refuse everyday requests and expectations (“demands”), argue with adults, become easily frustrated, and blame others for their own behavior.
  • Despite the challenges being very similar, the online narratives that supposedly underlie these behaviors are quite different between PDA and ODD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Pathological demand avoidance (PDA) has promptly become the prevailing explanation in online parenting communities for children with challenging behavior, while oppositional defiant disorder has taken a backseat.

Parents of both describe very similar challenges: kids who are highly emotionally reactive, refuse everyday requests and expectations (“demands”), argue with adults, become easily frustrated, and blame others for their own behavior.

Despite the challenges being very similar, the online narratives that supposedly underlie these behaviors are quite different between PDA and ODD. ODD is often portrayed on social media as willful, anger-driven behavior, while PDA is presented as an involuntary response to anxiety or a threat to autonomy.

It has been revealed that parents seem to gravitate to the second explanation because it offers a more compassionate perspective. Seeing our kids as scared invites us to comfort them, but seeing them as angry makes us feel we need to correct them.

An key distinction that gets lost in this discussion is that psychiatric diagnoses do not include proposed causes for the condition and instead describe patterns of symptoms and behaviors.

Sources indicate that for example, take major depressive disorder. The diagnostic criteria include sadness, hopelessness, loss of interest in formerly enjoyable activities, and so on, but the criteria do not include a “chemical imbalance.” The DSM or ICD don't include proposed causes because a clinician must give a diagnosis even if the underlying mechanisms are not well understood.

The same principle applies to ODD. The diagnosis describes patterns of argumentativeness and resistance to following adult directions, but, like every other diagnosis, it doesn’t require us to establish an underlying motivation or driver.

In a recent development, but maybe PDA really is driven by anxiety? Although this has not yet been established scientifically (it’s been proposed, not established), a child who meets the full diagnostic criteria for ODD can still receive that diagnosis. If the criteria for ODD don’t require anger to be the underlying cause, then identifying anxiety doesn’t automatically invalidate it.

Recent findings suggest that of course, we should continue to better understand possible underlying causes, including anxiety-driven avoidance. But “the behavior is driven by anxiety” is not, by itself, a reason to conclude that ODD isn’t an appropriate diagnosis.

The idea that PDA is driven by anxiety while ODD is driven by anger sounds pretty straightforward, but the evidence doesn’t support such a clear-cut distinction.

Children with ODD can also experience significant anxiety (Boylan and colleagues, 2007). Conversely, parents interviewed about children with PDA-type behavior also report that they are often angry (O’Nions and colleagues, 2018).

In a recent development, as I’ve proposed elsewhere (Sunseri, 2026b), anxiety might not drive demand avoidance at all. Instead, anxiety could very well be the natural byproduct of years of conflict and upsets with adult authority figures (“anxiety is the exhaust, not the engine”).

As a clinician, I might watch a child refuse to follow a direction, start yelling, and move into having a tantrum. However, I only know what the child did and can’t tell from the behaviors alone how much anxiety, anger, or both contributed to the upset.

I was curious to see how well represented PDA and ODD are on Facebook. I hypothesized that parents are being exposed to much more PDA content, so I searched for groups that were devoted exclusively to PDA or ODD. I was able to identify 44 PDA-related groups and only seven ODD-related groups.

According to recent reports, now imagine you’re a parent raising a very challenging child, and you want to learn more. You might join a group (or several), and you repeatedly find the same “explanation.” Support and community can help, of course, but if someone keeps reading the same information over and over, it will start to feel like a fact. Even if the parent first lands on an ODD group, invariably someone there will comment, “This sounds like PDA.”.

Sources indicate that PDA groups are also quite insular and often very hostile when someone challenges any of the prevailing narratives. As I have discussed elsewhere, researchers and clinicians are attacked and ultimately removed from the group (Sunseri, 2026a), leaving parents with the false impression that other views don’t exist.

According to recent reports, commercial influences have a strong incentive to maintain the “PDA is anxiety, and ODD is anger” argument: “Your child has a fundamentally different condition. Therapists don’t understand it, but I do. Conventional treatments don’t work, but I can help you.”.

According to recent reports, for the hundreds of PDA “coaches” advertising in these PDA groups, acknowledging that PDA and ODD are likely the same condition undercuts their business model. If well-researched and established treatments exist for kids who resist following directions, are highly emotionally reactive, and engage in near-constant conflict with others, why would a parent pay for their alternative?

Industry observers note that challenging the well-publicized commercialized narrative is similar to what my wife encountered working in public health; she and her colleagues tried to encourage families to adopt healthier eating habits. Tremendous resistance from well-funded, highly visible fast-food companies with a strong financial incentive drowned out voices advocating healthier alternatives. It’s hard to convince a kid to eat an apple when there’s a McDonald’s on every corner.

It’s important to note that there is truth in what parents say about traditional therapy not helping them and providers dismissing the seriousness of their child’s behavior. Treatment can fail when it is poorly delivered or adapts insufficiently. These kids are legitimately hard, and parents’ lived experiences are real, but an unsuccessful course of treatment does not establish that evidence-based approaches do not exist or that a coach selling a more reassuring story, free of any obligation to report measurable outcomes, is a better alternative.

Recent findings suggest that effective treatments do exist. Parent behavior training has demonstrated benefits for disruptive behavior and noncompliance in autistic children (Bearss and colleagues, 2015). Coaches routinely tell parents that “behavioral approaches don’t work with PDA,” but the right ones are highly effective.

Industry observers note that A 2026 review proposes a comprehensive, family-focused approach to addressing behavioral difficulties, anxiety, and family distress in autistic children (Shehu and Orhani, 2026). The authors recommend parent-mediated behavioral interventions as the treatment foundation, coupled with family-based CBT for co-occurring anxiety and systemic family therapy for communication and relationship difficulties.

Industry observers note that families don’t need to settle a debate about labels before seeking help for their child. They need real treatment guided by science, evidence, and measured outcomes, and not by presumed mechanisms pushed by commercial interests.

The question isn’t which explanation sounds better. It’s which approach actually helps your child.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that sharing is caring, even amongst aquariums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Boston’s New England Aquarium recently shipped a very crucial package. But it wasn’t exactly an early Christmas gift. The team shipped 22 lookdown fish across the country via air transport. And they’re not the only institution that routinely packs fishes up and sends them elsewhere. The NEA are part of a group of aquariums where each member specializes in raising certain species on behalf of the entire group. They then send the fish to the other member aquariums.

In a recent development, “By working together, we are able to raise more fish, and develop aquaculture practices to successfully raise more species, including some that have never been raised before, like copper/glassy sweepers, blue chromis, and brown chromis,” Monika Schmück, manager of sustainability in the fishes department at the Fresh England Aquarium, tells Popular Science. “We typically raise 500-1000 fish annually and distribute them to over 15 institutions on average each year.”.

Recent findings suggest that sharing is caring, even amongst aquariums. When it comes time for the fish’s journey, the team needs to decide whether to use air or ground transport. To do this, they consider factors including external temperature, the weight of the shipment, and access to an airport at the destination. Depending on the time of the year, cargo holding and ground transport trucks can experience extreme temperatures, Schmück points out.

According to recent reports, if it’s a large shipment, the New England Aquarium usually goes for air cargo, whereas smaller shipments are easier to deliver with ground transportation. Overall, ground transportation is the easiest strategy because it doesn’t have to take into account the location of airports.

On a smaller scale, moving a fish isn’t as easy as sticking a cat into a crate. In terms of the container in which the animal will travel, the biggest consideration is the size of remarked animal, which determines how much water it needs.

“Since fish must be transported in water, and water is heavy, the design of a fish transport first must address how to safely move the required volume of water to keep the fish safe and secure during the process,” Schmück explains.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the fundamentals of fish transport are mostly consistent no matter the species. Experts need to make sure that the water chemistry is good during the entire trip and that other environmental conditions are appropriate for the traveling species and remain stable.

  • The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) declared on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 people have a upcoming symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) declared on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S. labels for Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity, Mounjaro, and Zepbound already warn about diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye disease, according to each drug’s prescribing information.The two conditions affect different parts of the eye. Diabetic retinopathy damages tiny blood vessels in the retina, the layer at the back of the eye that senses light, according to the National Eye Institute. NAION damages the optic nerve when it doesn’t get enough blood, according to the FDA’s announcement.Mihail Zilbermint, MD, director of endocrine hospitalists at Johns Hopkins, told Healthline he hasn’t seen NAION in his patients. He has seen vision worsen in some people after they start a GLP-1.“But we believe that’s probably related to rapid improvement in their sugar control, which can also be seen in someone who is starting insulin,” Zilbermint stated.

A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.

The study found a higher risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, than in people prescribed other diabetes or weight-loss drugs.The authors wrote that more research is needed to determine whether semaglutide causes NAION.Joseph F. Rizzo III, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, served as the study’s corresponding author.

In a 2024 podcast, Rizzo stated he and a resident saw three patients with NAION who were taking semaglutide for about a week.“And because NAION is a fairly uncommon disorder in the general population, the fact that we had three within a relatively short period of time led me to suspect that there was a higher risk of developing NAION in patients on semaglutide,” Rizzo said. The FDA analyzed clinical trials for multiple GLP-1 drugs and noted that NAION cases were reported with every GLP-1 on the market, according to its announcement. Those findings led the FDA to require the warning for the entire drug class, the agency told Healthline.

Sources indicate that about 70% to 80% of people with NAION first notice vision loss when they wake up, according to StatPearls. The FDA listed these symptoms:.

No treatment has been proven to reverse vision loss from NAION, according to StatPearls.

“Patients experiencing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye should contact their healthcare professional immediately and should not stop their medication without consulting their provider first,” the FDA told Healthline.

In the announcement, the agency told doctors to promptly refer patients with suspected NAION to an ophthalmologist.

The FDA listed these possible risk factors for NAION:.

The FDA told Healthline that many people who take GLP-1s also have these conditions, which made reports of NAION in GLP-1 customers “challenging” to interpret.

Across 126 clinical trials, the FDA found about 6 NAION cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for a year, and about 4 per 100,000 people taking a placebo or another diabetes drug for a year.In real-world data, NAION was more common with GLP-1s than with one type of diabetes pill, but the FDA found no significant increase compared with another type, the agency told Healthline.Zilbermint mentioned patients who saw the news have worried about losing their vision. He tells them that “many of the serious harms, including the potential harm of NAION, are rare.”“The overall risk is still very small,” he said.

Regulators in other countries have added NAION warnings, mostly for semaglutide:.

The FDA told Healthline the benefits of GLP-1s “continue to outweigh their risks when used as directed.”The FDA has also approved some GLP-1s to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, and treat sleep apnea and a type of liver disease.Zilbermint remarked that “for most of my patients with obesity, diabetes and heart disease, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.”“But we definitely have to decide patient by patient,” he added.

The labeling change applies to these medications, according to the FDA’s announcement:.

As of publication, the FDA’s online label database did not yet show the fresh warning on the drugs’ labels.

Breaking: Honda Recalling Thousands of S2000s for Potential Fuel Leak

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (289 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s not too often we get upcoming recalls for older cars like the Honda S2000, but today is one of those days.
  • The reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda indicates this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall.
  • Honda states that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material.

It’s not too often we get upcoming recalls for older cars like the Honda S2000, but today is one of those days. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Honda is recalling 16,387 S2000 roadsters from the 2004–20005 model years, the first two years of the AP2 refresh. A quick look at the sales figures for those years seems to suggest that means all (or close to all) S2000s from those years are part of the recall population.

The reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda indicates this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall. The problem with manufacturing relates to whether or not it was built with brazing material at the joint-to-flange connection. With the part being a push-to-fit part, Honda says this lack of material could cause the connection to become loose and separate.

Honda states that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material. These parts were shipped and potentially installed in S2000s. Honda estimates the percentage of cars with the defect is 1 percent. There won’t be many warning signs before it’s too late to continue driving, but Honda says stalling, a misfire, fuel odor and an inability to start the engine are all symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that as of now, Honda indicates there are no injuries or deaths related to this glitch. Those with cars in the recall range will have to bring their convertibles into the Honda dealer for the remedy. Once there, it will receive a new and improved fuel flange joint assembly free of charge.

‘Vibe coding’ is risky: Here’s why and what to do about it

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to rapid advances in AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, “vibe coding” is very much a possibility for anyone: Just use natural language to explain what you want a program to do, and the AI will put it together for you.
  • This has led non-programmers to quickly create their own sites and apps, and you’ll find a multitude of examples online.
  • Recent findings suggest that vibe-coding gadgets can lead to some impressive demonstrations of AI’s current capabilities, but is it wise to try it at home on the devices you use every day?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to rapid advances in AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, “vibe coding” is very much a possibility for anyone: Just use natural language to explain what you want a program to do, and the AI will put it together for you.

This has led non-programmers to quickly create their own sites and apps, and you’ll find a multitude of examples online. Vibe coding has extended to hardware too—whether it’s people hacking into their 1994 Cherokee Jeep or repurposing an Amazon Kindle.

Recent findings suggest that vibe-coding gadgets can lead to some impressive demonstrations of AI’s current capabilities, but is it wise to try it at home on the devices you use every day? Probably not, and we’ll explain why here.

Sources indicate that if you’ve never used an AI app to vibe code—or used an AI app at all—then you might be wondering what all the talk about vibe coding actually means. It’s the widely used, informal term for prompting an AI chatbot to create a program: Maybe you want a phone app to track your exercise, for example, or a simple game you can play in your browser.

As long as your ambitions aren’t too grand—you’re not going to get GTA VI out of this anytime soon—your AI engine of choice will produce a slick, usable, custom-made app for you within a few minutes. If there are any bugs or challenges (and there often are), then you can use follow-up prompts to get rid of them.

It has been revealed that while the end results might need a bit of finessing and don’t match up to what a team of professional software developers can do, it’s incredible to think that AI now enables anyone to write apps of their own, no manual coding required. Need a registration website for your sports club or an app to track trains at your local station? Just ask for it.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not to say there aren’t downsides to vibe coding, though, which we’ll get to next. AI code isn’t always the most reliable or efficient, and you need to be aware of its limitations—and put safeguards in place to make sure there’s no danger of vibe-coded apps causing challenges for other hardware and software.

As TechCrunch reports, television sets are common targets for some vibe-coded tinkering. People are using code produced by AI apps to simplify the app launchers, take out sponsored content and advertising, and turn off some of the aggressive tracking features that come with modern-day TVs, for example.

Industry observers note that here’s the problem: While the AI app developers don’t often mention it, AI code often comes with bugs and unintended consequences attached, and if you don’t understand what you’re coding, then you can’t fix it. That’s not so much of an glitch if you’re trying to get a custom soccer score tracker running in your browser, but if you’re suddenly bricking your main TV, then that is a problem.

In a recent development, the operating systems on TVs—as well as tablets, laptops, speakers, fridges, and other gadgets—can be complex, and AIs will often guess at what the right approach is if they don’t know for sure. You risk breaking key functionality, creating latest bugs while trying to fix existing ones, and leaving security vulnerabilities open that hackers can target.

Of course it’s easy to see the appeal of an ad-free TV that runs faster than before, but is it worth opening up your television set to malware? Or not being able to use the Netflix app for reasons you can’t fathom? Or one day finding that it’s stuck in an endless loop between shutting down and powering up? These are the risks of vibe coding.

Different categories of devices work in different ways, but you’ll often find that there are more reliable ways of customizing your hardware than relying on something you’ve vibe-coded yourself. When it comes to TVs, for example, there are often alternative launchers available, such as Projectivy Launcher for Google TV models, which is ad-free and offers a ton of customization options.

For routers, there’s something like OpenWrt, which is built and maintained by a large enthusiast community. It lets you do all sorts of things with compatible routers, including blocking ads and trackers, customizing which devices can access the network and when, monitoring bandwidth, and integrating a VPN at the router level.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking to do more with your smart home devices, then Home Assistant is definitely worth a look. The popular alternative smart home system management software gives you much more control over your devices and what you can do with them than the comparable apps offered by Amazon, Google, and Apple.

Industry observers note that you’re still putting your faith in third-party code that you haven’t personally written—but these projects are managed by capable software developers and backed by massive user communities that monitor issues like security and compatibility. When it comes to keeping your gadgets usable, they’re the safer bet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage.
  • According to recent reports, but Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea.
  • It has been revealed that that's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage. It makes sense that it will not be driven every day; however, often times cars like this are not really driven at all. They spend their entire lives in climate-controlled garages, tucked beneath soft covers. And when the car in question is something like a one-of-25 C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, the temptation to preserve it as a collectible is understandable.

According to recent reports, but Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea. He wants his customers to get behind the wheel and drive. "We prefer to sell our cars to people that actually use them," Muller told me during an interview at Retromobile New York. "Because that's what I made them for. To drive the hell out of them.".

It has been revealed that that's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey. Particularly when that car is the fresh C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, which looks as much like a piece of fine jewelry as an 800-horsepower road rocket. Unfortunately, Muller admits that many of Spyker's previous creations haven't enjoyed particularly active lives.

According to recent reports, "Many of our cars, of the 252 we made so far, have just ended up in dungeons, in vaults, in spaces where nobody will ever see them," Muller noted. He's hoping to change that by organizing more owner events and encouraging customers to spend time enjoying their cars; Spyker has joined the Supercar Owners Circle, a global network of car collectors, and is planning gatherings in Europe and the United States.

According to recent reports, the company is also in a position where it can be selective about who gets its cars. According to Muller, all 25 Preliator XXV Coupés sold during their debut at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering in August. Every single one was snapped up in a day. "I've never seen anything like that in my entire life," he said. Spyker intends to build 25 Spyders and 25 Sedancas in 2028, he added, once production of the Coupés is complete next year.

Recent findings suggest that who is buying these cars has changed dramatically over the last quarter century. "In 2000, my typical customer was a fifty-five to sixty-year-old industrialist—old money, car collector, very astute buyer," Muller explained. "Fast forward twenty five years. Your average age is thirty-five years. Tech investor. Huge collection. Knows his cars completely. But nobody asks how much it is.".

Muller says approximately 40 percent of his new buyers are existing or former Spyker owners, and roughly 80 percent of the new cars are expected to go to the United States. But no matter how old the buyer is or where they live, Muller wants them to drive the cars. This makes sense when you understand his approach to engineering; The new car has no massive infotainment screens or hybrid systems, and electronic intervention is largely limited to essential safety features like ABS and stability control.

In a recent development, “If you mis-shift in a Spyker and you drive two hundred miles an hour and you shift to second gear, you blow up the engine," Muller remarked. "And I think it has to be that way in Spyker world." For Spyker, the connection between driver and machine is more important than chasing lap records, acceleration figures and electronic nannies. "If you don't like that, buy something else," he added. "If not, man up—drive a Spyker.".

Recent findings suggest that another way to demonstrate that these cars are meant to be driven is to get the brand back into racing. Muller revealed that Spyker is taking steps toward returning to professional endurance competition. The tech giant competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans eight times, most recently in 2010. Naturally, I asked whether another trip to Le Mans might be in Spyker's future.

"Absolutely," Muller remarked. "We'd love to go back in racing." Muller notes Spyker is preparing to re-enter endurance racing, although he stopped short of announcing a timeline, championship, or confirmed race entry. He certainly likes the idea of seeing his latest creation on the track. More importantly, he's already started putting people in place to make it happen.

"I actually hired my former GT2 race director again," Muller stated. "He started a week ago today.".

#155689. Industry News: How to Swiftly Weed Out Manipulators When Dating

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1012 w)

Industry News: How to Swiftly Weed Out Manipulators When Dating

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the dating world is full of tricksters.
  • Recent findings suggest that ordinarily, empathy is what allows you to remain close to the people that you care about.
  • However, in the dating world, some people may have a victim mentality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

It has been revealed that the dating world is full of tricksters. If you are a person with emotional intelligence, several of your EI tendencies may backfire with a certain type of person. This may be especially true when your heart is involved and you long to be loved. Four EI qualities can work against you when you are dating; empathy, perspective-taking, vulnerability, and positivity. Educating yourself on how and when to rein them in may help you quickly weed out a manipulator.

Recent findings suggest that ordinarily, empathy is what allows you to remain close to the people that you care about. You open your heart and your mind to better understand them. Thinking about how they must feel in their situation allows you to resonate and really “feel for them.” When you convey this understanding to them, they usually feel less alone, connected to you because you get it, and a bit better. It can be transformative.

However, in the dating world, some people may have a victim mentality. They believe that their life has been harder than anyone else’s and they identify a list of past hardships to elicit your empathy. Yet, instead of integrating your empathy to gain emotional relief, they indirectly invite you to “fix” things for them. Often this requires that you sacrifice something that is important to you.

Although you think that they are opening up when they tell you their tales of woe, they may not be. A person with a victim narrative rarely talks about how they grappled with difficult and nuanced emotions to recover. Nor do they identify any profound insight or a silver lining. This may signify that they did not actually recover from their past difficulties but rather prefer to use them to dodge accountability in a current relationship, so be careful. The sad narratives can result in you feeling like their life has been harder than yours, so you must give more to them and the relationship. Yet, after a while, you realize that you are being exploited.

It is key to note that you too have been through your share of trauma. However, if you have emotional intelligence, you are someone who can recognize, identify, and process deep and uncomfortable emotions. Your self-awareness and ability to deeply reflect on your experiences allow you to eventually recover, grow, and become stronger. A person who lacks these abilities tends to use their past difficulties as a license to manipulate others in the present.

It has been revealed that if you are someone who possesses emotional intelligence, you also look at different perspectives without even recognizing that you are. It’s almost automatic. Your desire to truly understand the people that you care about drives you to look at things from their viewpoint. Unfortunately, there are many people in the dating world who do not take perspective. It can be deceiving because their unwavering belief that they are always right in the context of their interpersonal relationships makes them appear uber confident. Yet, this may not be the case. This individual may be too insecure to be wrong, so they refuse to look at things from your angle. They continually espouse their viewpoint as correct and dismiss and ignore your opinion about the matter. This can create an imbalance of power in the relationship because you are always trying to understand their perspective, and they rarely consider yours. To avoid the disagreements that this unfairness creates, you often acquiesce and continually surrender to what they say and want. As the relationship progresses, they gain more and more emotional control over you.

As an EI person, your vulnerability is normally a strength because you are secure enough to truly open up to someone fresh, but it can backfire with a problematic person. Since you are not defensive or emotionally walled off, you are comfortable talking about your insecurities, uncomfortable emotions, scars, fears, and idiosyncrasies. In fact, you long for closeness and are excited at the thought of becoming close with someone new. However, if you don’t keep an eye on this tendency at the beginning of a relationship, you may open up too soon and with too much personal and private information.

If your date is a problematic person, they may use this data to hurt you during an argument. They may also weaponize it to zap your confidence because they want you to feel “small” so they feel “big.” This creates another type of imbalance in the relationship because their self-narrative is absent of any deep and emotional self-disclosures. They simply describe a litany of hardships. So, now they know all of your insecurities, but you know none of theirs. To add insult to injury, they may glibly reference a general insecurity to excuse a wrongdoing or to exploit your empathy.

In a recent development, lastly, as an EI person, you tend to see the good in people. You are a glass-half-full individual, and you long for harmony and good vibes in your relationships-- and this is a remarkable quality in most situations. However, when you are in the dating world, it can cause problems. Your positivity can tempt you to dismiss a upcoming person’s red flags and thoughtless behaviors, which can create inequality in the relationship. You are “all in,” and you give as much as possible to this person while they give far less, emotionally, and are very critical of you.

In a recent development, everyone is on their best behavior at the beginning of a dating relationship, so do not give a fresh person too much credit too early. Be aware of your emotionally intelligent tendencies and rein them in when you need to.

You can find more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist: Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, at Work, and In Life.

#155688. Industry News: The best way to pack a suitcase, according to science

Industry News: The best way to pack a suitcase, according to science

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1491 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that while recently packing for an overseas excursion, I stuffed every spare space I could find in my carry-on.
  • To find out how best to pack according to science, Popular Science turned to Anne McAlpin, a travel expert and author of the book, Pack it Up: the Essential Guide to Smart Travel.
  • Many carry-on bags have “ruts” or internal grooves to accommodate a recessed trolley handle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while recently packing for an overseas excursion, I stuffed every spare space I could find in my carry-on. I used what I call the “Mary Poppins” packing method: willing myself to believe that whatever I wanted to put in my luggage would fit, regardless of the size of the object or the size of my bag. Somehow my system worked, but when I arrived at my destination and unzipped my bag, everything within it exploded onto the floor. “There’s gotta be a better way,” I thought.

To find out how best to pack according to science, Popular Science turned to Anne McAlpin, a travel expert and author of the book, Pack it Up: the Essential Guide to Smart Travel. Over the course of her lifetime, McAlpin has estimated she’s packed—and unpacked—more than 25,000 times! She’s a whiz at minimizing dead space, maximizing volume, and keeping clothes looking more like they came off a closet hanger than straight out of a laundry bin.

Many carry-on bags have “ruts” or internal grooves to accommodate a recessed trolley handle. This handle uses two narrow metal poles that retract straight into the middle or sides of the interior lining, causing the interior surface of the suitcase to be uneven.

Recent findings suggest that “If you don’t have a flat foundation, make one,” claims McAlpin. Having a flat foundation maximizes space, prevents wrinkles, and adds stability to your bag. To do this, consider evening out the space between ruts with packing or compression cubes. “You can put all of your underwear into a compression cube,” a small bag made of breathable nylon or polyester mesh used in part to organize items, and then place it between the ruts. This will even out the bottom of a hard-shell suitcase. Flexible items such as toiletry kits and rolled-up socks can help to form this base layer as well. “I then pack my clothing on top of that flat foundation.”.

McAlpin puts her shoes (she usually packs two pairs and wears a third) towards the bottom of the suitcase so that the weight is on the wheels. “You don’t want to put your heavy items on the top of the inside of your suitcase,” she notes. “This will cause it to constantly topple.”.

When it comes to clothing, McAlpin rolls some items and flat packs others. “I call it interlayering,” she says.

For example, with pants, rather than folding them to stack in a pile, McAlpin lays each pair out along its natural creases as if she were going to put them on a hanger. Then, she places them in her suitcase: waistband at the top of one side of the bag, legs dangling out the other side of the bag. They’re not folded, but laid out straight. This way, McAlpin can then wrap them around the rolled items that she’ll later place on top of them.

Sources indicate that she does the same with cotton shirts, sundresses—anything that might wrinkle. With each item, McAlpin alternates the direction, so that there are no two waistbands or shirt collars bulking up one side of the suitcase.

“I then roll my knit items and synthetic things that don’t wrinkle as much. I roll them up like Tootsie Rolls and I place them side by side,” in the middle of the laid-out items. While folding clothes and stacking them leaves pockets of air both inside the folds and within the layers, rolling wraps fabrics into a smooth, tight cylinder, which reduces the overall amount of space each item uses. It’s the best of both worlds! Your laid-out items aren’t as wrinkled and your wrinkle-resistant items are more tightly packed. This allows for more room in your suitcase overall.

Sources indicate that when McAlpin has all her rolled items tightly packed together, she takes the pant legs and skirts that are still hanging off the sides of the suitcase, and “bends them up and over the ‘roll bar’ I’ve made of sweaters, pajamas, and sweats.” This helps avoid the knee creases that come when you’re simply folding pants. It also keeps items compact, and is a game-changer when it comes to unpacking. You can just lift all of the interlayered items out of your suitcase in one fell swoop.

Industry observers note that fill up empty space. For example, McAlpin says that if you’re a couple packing together, you may be able to slide a woman’s sandal right into a man’s shoe, or at least use the shoe’s interior cavity to store phone chargers, socks, or small items like earrings and even an eyeglasses case. Not only is it a space-saver, but filling up unused space prevents transit damage by keeping items inside from shifting.

Stuff the corners of a suitcase with socks, rolled-up t-shirts, etc, “because all those awkward corners offer prime packing space,” says McAlpin. Filling up those pockets also distributes structural stress throughout the bag, helping to keep features like zippers and fabric intact during excessive handling.

Sources indicate that why do our ears pop on a plane? An audiologist explains.

Why do we put seatbacks up for landing? An aviation expert explains.

Another trick: laying belts around the luggage perimeter so that they’re easier to find.

Industry observers note that to keep things condensed and organized, McAlpin suggests compression cubes. These small bags feature two zippers: a main zipper that closes the cube like a standard bag, and a second perimeter zipper that pulls the cube’s top and bottom panels closer together, squeezing out excess air and reducing volume. Compression cubes help eliminate air pockets that come with traditional folding and can reduce the volume of soft clothes like T-shirts and pants up to 30 percent.

Another option: roll-up compression bags. These pump-free, vacuum-free storage bags use one-way pressure valves to push air out, cutting volume by up to 80 percent. “I use these for laundry,” states McAlpin, because they temporarily block odors.

According to recent reports, “They’re like an industrial Ziploc bag,” she says, and great for bulky items like a fleece jacket. But use them sparingly. Roll sacks are typically made of plastic and cause a lot more wrinkles than traditional compression cubes.

McAlpin carries dry laundry sheets and a two-gallon Ziploc bag for washing clothes. “The bag doesn’t take up any room, and then I can wash my socks and underwear without worrying if I’ve left any toothpaste in the sink.”.

According to recent reports, mcAlpin states her packing “3:1 ratio” (three tops to every bottom) has “changed people’s lives.” She packs nine tops and three bottoms, and everything mixes and matches. “I base everything around two colors,” she says, “like a black and a tan,” and then throws in an occasional splash of color.

Recent findings suggest that this works, says McAlpin, because human memory registers outfits based on what’s closest to the head and face. And while she travels with three pairs of shoes, each one should be for something different. For example, runners for long walks, sandals for the beach, and loafers for evenings.

As for the bag itself, McAlpin notes four-wheel bags (spinner luggage) are a must. Not only are they easy to maneuver through packed terminals and airplane aisles, the ability to push the bag upright beside you keeps your arm in a neutral, bent-elbow position. This places less stress on your wrists, shoulders, and lower back compared to pulling a two-wheel bag behind you, and plays a substantial role in easing ergonomic strain.

Recent findings suggest that they’re also ideal for stacking, since they stay upright. Think about it, says McAlpin. “When you pack your heavy tote bag on top of your suitcase, it’s the bag, not your shoulders, that’s carrying the weight.”.

Ultimately, the idea is to make use of all your space, keep items from bumping around inside your suitcase and (if possible) wrinkle-free, and to not throw out your back in the process.

In a recent development, of course, when it comes to finding room for souvenirs, there’s always the Mary Poppins packing method. But after talking with McAlpin, I’ve been using her method exclusively. My clothes, formerly creased, rumpled, and crinkled, are now decidedly wrinkle-free!

Breaking: 1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.
  • According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.
  • However, fresh research published in the November 2026 concern of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.

According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.

However, fresh research published in the November 2026 concern of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.

In fact, having a history of reacting to peanuts and positive allergy testing on their own may not be sufficient to diagnose a peanut allergy for many infants.

The study’s authors suggest that a threshold oral food challenge — in which the child is given increasing amounts of the suspected food allergen under medical supervision to look for an allergic reaction — should be routinely considered to help confirm peanut allergy.

This additional testing could safely prevent children who are not allergic to peanuts from undergoing unnecessary treatment with oral immunotherapy.

It could also spare families from burdensome food restrictions and allergy precautions.

The researchers’ goal was to evaluate the accuracy and safety of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Path to Tolerance (ADAPT) peanut oral immunotherapy program, which was established in 2024 at 10 public children’s hospitals across Australia.

This program provides a standardized approach to evaluating and treating infants with suspected peanut allergies.

The study included infants who had experienced a mild to moderate reaction to peanut before 12 months of age and had evidence of peanut sensitization through allergy testing.

Researchers reviewed medical records to examine how accurately the program’s approach identified peanut allergies and whether it could safely guide treatment.

Sources indicate that A key part of the evaluation was a threshold oral food challenge. The challenge involved up to seven doses, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams of peanut protein.

Medical teams monitored the infants for reactions and provided treatment when necessary.

According to recent reports, researchers reviewed records from April 2024 through October 2025. During that period, 1,275 infants were assessed through the program, and 778 underwent an oral food challenge.

The researchers also examined allergy test results and whether infants who reacted during the challenges could begin oral immunotherapy at an appropriate starting dose.

At the time of the oral food challenge, the infants had a median age of 13 months.

Of the 778 infants who underwent an oral food challenge, 507 (65.2%) had an allergic reaction.

However, 271 (34.8%) did not react to peanut during the supervised test, despite having a history of a previous reaction and positive allergy test results.

These findings suggest that relying on medical history and allergy tests alone may lead some infants to be labeled with a peanut allergy when they can actually tolerate the food.

Among the infants who reacted during the challenges, 61 experienced anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. This represented 12% of infants with a positive challenge and 7.8% of all infants who underwent testing. Medical teams safely managed these severe allergic reactions.

Researchers also found that infants who reacted to peanut generally had higher skin prick test results and Ara h 2-specific IgE levels than those who did not react.

However, these test results did not reliably indicate how much peanut would trigger a reaction or how severe that reaction would be.

Of the 394 infants who began peanut oral immunotherapy, 384 (97.5%) successfully started treatment at a dose below the amount that had triggered a reaction during their food challenge.

The researchers say these findings support considering supervised oral food challenges to confirm suspected peanut allergies before starting treatment or recommending long-term avoidance.

Erin Banta, MD, a board certified allergist and immunologist who treats both children and adults at Latitude Food Allergy Care in Great Neck, New York, stated these findings are significant because they provide evidence for early use of oral food challenges in infants with peanut reactions.

“In those with mild-moderate prior reactions to peanut, early oral food challenge may allow for either delabeling of food allergy (in 1/3 of the patients in this study) or diagnosis of food allergy,” she told Healthline.

Banta, who wasn’t involved in the study, added that early delabeling takes a significant burden off the patient and their family.

“On the other hand,” she explained, “early diagnosis allows for early initiation of treatment with oral immunotherapy at a time in the patient’s life associated with the greatest success rates.”.

It has been revealed that banta further noted that the study offers different pathways for oral immunotherapy based on the patient’s reaction threshold. This means that some patients may be able to complete treatment more quickly due to their individual threshold dose.

Lindsey Forstie, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with clinical training and experience in allergy and asthma care at Carefree Allergy in Phoenix, AZ, added that while further evaluation may be needed to confirm a peanut allergy diagnosis, it’s important for parents not to try introducing peanuts at home.

“Instead, they should speak with their pediatrician or allergist about appropriate testing and whether a supervised food challenge is safe and necessary,” she said.

According to Forstie, who was also not part of the study, the goal is to avoid unnecessary food restrictions while also keeping children safe.

Industry observers note that “The key message is that not every positive allergy test means a child has a food allergy,” she told Healthline. “Accurate diagnosis helps protect children while allowing those who are not allergic to enjoy a more normal, less restrictive diet.”.
