📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Red Dog Mine in Alaska burns about 40,000 gallons of diesel a day to keep one of the world’s largest zinc mines running, and now, an 8.8-megawatt (MW) solar farm and battery storage will help cut that fuel use.

According to recent reports, the Alaska Energy Authority’s board unanimously approved a nearly $5 million loan for the project through its Power Project Fund. Tugliq Red Dog1 will build, own, and operate the roughly $35 million solar project and sell the electricity to mine operator Teck Alaska. The state’s loan review claims site work began in June and expects the solar and storage to come online in October 2028.

In a recent development, red Dog sits about 105 miles north of the Arctic Circle, on land owned by NANA, an Iñupiat-owned Alaska Native corporation. The array would be larger than any solar farm operating in Alaska today, as KOTZ’s Desiree Hagen reported for Alaska Public Media. Hagen reported that the aims call for more than 15,000 panels across around 30 acres.

It has been revealed that the mine gets all its power from on-site diesel generators. In summer, it can draw so much electricity that Teck has to cut power elsewhere at the site. The solar array and the 8.8 MW, 15 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery will give the operator another source of power during those crunches.

The state of Alaska expects the solar and storage project to cover about 5% of the zinc mine’s electricity needs under its current operating initiative. The project could do even more after mining ends, covering about 90% of the site’s annual electricity needs.

Cost to import sun to a remote Alaskan village 0, cost to import diesel quite high.

Sources indicate that A 500W panel weighs 60 lbs about the same as 9 gallons of diesel. 500W panel generates 750kwh of electricity a year each and every year for 20 years. 9 gallons of diesel gives you 350kwh of thermal energy which yields varying amounts of desired output.

Recent findings suggest that teck expects the mine’s existing deposits to support operations through 2031, and it’s studying whether to develop two nearby deposits. If that expansion goes ahead, the state projects the solar and battery project would cover about 3% of the larger operation’s electricity needs. If mining ends, demand will drop sharply, but the site will still need electricity for cleanup and long-term water treatment.

#155684. How a red wolf gets a checkup

How a red wolf gets a checkup

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (366 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Annual human checkups are relatively straightforward.
  • We’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam.
  • “The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Annual human checkups are relatively straightforward. You hop onto the exam table, stick your tongue out, stare straight ahead as the doctor beams light into your eyes, let them tap their small hammer against that wildly uncomfortable spot under your kneecap, etc. But for wildlife, it’s a whole other experience.

We’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam. But what about another favorite carnivore—wolves? According to Vicki Scharfberg, from Roger Williams Park Zoo & Carousel Village in Rhode Island, the annual wellness examination for red wolves (Canis rufus) is not that different from a pet dog’s annual veterinary visit.

“The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.

Sources indicate that the checkup includes a physical examination at the wolf enclosure or the zoo veterinary hospital, bloodwork, vaccinations, heartworm prevention care, and if necessary, parasite treatment. A social media post by Roger Williams Park Zoo showcases their red wolf named Frye thoroughly knocked out on the exam table, undergoing an oral exam, among other things.

In a recent development, the team uses the bloodwork to check on the wolf’s organs and screen for heartworm disease. Interestingly, their vaccines are the exact same ones veterinarians give to domestic dogs for rabies, distemper, parvovirus, and leptospirosis.

Heartworm prevention treatment involves a long-acting 12 month injection. Heartworm disease is caused by grossly long worms called heartworms that take up residence in an animals’ heart, lungs, and related blood vessels. This parasitic condition triggers severe lung disease, heart failure, and damages other organs. Heartworm is potentially fatal, and in addition to wolves can also impact animals including dogs, cats, ferrets, foxes, and humans.

“If something abnormal is found on the examination, we follow up with additional diagnostics like x-rays, ultrasound, or a consult with a veterinary specialist (dentist, cardiologist, etc),” Scharfberg concludes.

#155682. How to Know When It’s Time to End Therapy

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1114 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

How to Know When It’s Time to End Therapy

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • Industry observers note that "Got it.
  • That was the message I received from my therapist of two years after I sent him a thoughtful email to terminate our work together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

Industry observers note that "Got it. Best wishes for your continued personal development and your career.”.

That was the message I received from my therapist of two years after I sent him a thoughtful email to terminate our work together.

After our last session didn’t go well, I questioned whether I wanted a termination session. Something inside me told me it was the last time I’d see him. I had brought up something he had done that didn’t feel good and had reenacted a feeling of abandonment.

After I left, I remember thinking, “He didn’t handle that well.”.

It has been revealed that I realize now that the part of me that didn’t want to have a final termination session in person had intuitively sensed his response. His email confirmed what I had felt, and I realized I was protecting myself from having to experience his coldness in person.

Being a therapist who is also looking for a therapist has given me a deeper appreciation for how crucial the therapeutic relationship is.

Recent findings suggest that shortly after, I consulted with another therapist. When he asked about my past therapy, I told him how it had ended. Rather than acknowledge how it might have felt to receive that response from a therapist I’d worked with for two years, he noted he could understand my therapist’s response because “maybe he still had more work to do with me.”.

According to recent reports, maybe he had more work to do with me, I thought, confused. It was my therapy, not my therapist’s. I was making a decision about what was best for me.

When clients are brave enough to recognize when something isn’t working and communicate that to their therapist, they may still question themselves, especially if they grew up in families where their feelings and needs weren’t acknowledged.

In a recent development, there were many times when I thought about terminating with my therapist, and a few times when I consulted with other therapists during our work together. I’ve come to recognize a pattern of staying in situations and relationships longer than I want to or should.

I think many of us have a hard time knowing when to end relationships, including our therapeutic relationships. We may question whether we’re being too sensitive, whether we’re expecting too much, or whether something that didn’t feel good was our own concern to work through.

If you’re in therapy and questioning whether you’re with the right therapist, it doesn’t automatically mean you’re not. It could be an opportunity for you and your therapist to check in about your goals and how things are going. I had done that with my own therapist, too. More than once, I told him I had a desire for him to pursue me more and ask questions about my past, but he didn’t seem to understand what I was trying to communicate. That was part of what contributed to my decision to leave.

Clients should be able to bring all of themselves into therapy and say how they feel, even when what they say might feel personal to the therapist. That’s part of our work as therapists. We have to be willing to examine our own reactions and understand how our expectations and unresolved feelings can influence the therapeutic relationship. In clinical terms, it’s working with transference and countertransference.

Our clients’ therapy is about them, not us.

Yes, therapy is a relationship, and we are part of that relationship. But when we aren’t aware of our own reactions, we can perpetuate the very wounds our clients are trying to repair.

Research supports the importance of paying attention to the therapeutic relationship, particularly when something goes wrong. A 2018 meta-analysis by Catherine Eubanks, J. Christopher Muran, and Jeremy Safran found a moderate association between successful rupture repair and positive psychotherapy outcomes.

The American Psychological Association also emphasizes that therapists should respond to signs of a rupture without becoming defensive, acknowledge their own contributions when appropriate, and examine their emotional reactions through self-awareness, consultation, and supervision.

Industry observers note that A rupture doesn’t automatically mean therapy should end. Sometimes working through a difficult interaction can become an notable part of the work. But repair requires a therapist who is willing to listen, take responsibility, and understand the impact of their behavior. Clients shouldn’t have to convince their therapist that their experience matters.

It has been revealed that therapy can offer us a reparative experience with endings. Many of us don’t know how to end relationships well. We may avoid difficult conversations, stay longer than we want, or leave without expressing what we feel. A thoughtful termination gives us an opportunity to reflect on the relationship, acknowledge what we’ve gained, express what didn’t work, and say goodbye.

For some clients, having a therapist who can make room for those conversations can be an notable part of their healing.

When clients choose to end therapy, it’s our responsibility to support their decisions, even when we have our own feelings about the ending. A therapist might feel disappointed, sad, or hurt. Those feelings deserve attention, but they’re the therapist’s responsibility to work through, not the client’s.

Sources indicate that if a therapist believes a client would benefit from another session or a different kind of ending, they can express that and invite a conversation. They also have to respect the client’s choice.

If you find yourself looking for another therapist while still working with your current one, it may be worth asking why. If you consistently feel missed, misunderstood, or as though your therapist is making assumptions about your experience, those are things worth bringing into the room. They may become important areas of exploration.

But if you can’t raise your concerns without offending your therapist, or repeated attempts to communicate what you need don’t lead to greater understanding, it may be time to consider ending the relationship.

You don’t need your therapist’s permission to end therapy or to prove your reasons are good enough. Therapy can help you develop a stronger relationship with yourself, including the ability to recognize when something isn’t working and make decisions that support your well-being.

Sometimes trusting yourself to know when to leave is part of the work.

Eubanks, C. F., Muran, J. C., & Safran, J. D. (2018). Alliance rupture repair: A meta-analysis. Psychotherapy, 55(4), 508–519. https://doi.org/10.1037/pst0000185.

According to recent reports, american Psychological Association. (2021). Professional practice guidelines for evidence-based psychological practice in health care. https://www.apa.org/about/policy/psychological-practice-health-care.pdf.

  • Sources indicate that electric-first is also the go-to-market strategy—at least in Europe.
  • See all results for upcoming 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA-Class EV for sale near 85705.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at the debut of the redesigned Mercedes-Benz GLA, company chairman Ola Källenius noted, “The ICE [internal-combustion engine] world and the BEV [battery-electric vehicle] world have come together.” And that’s true: Apart from their grilles, the gas-engine GLA and the first-ever GLA EV are virtually indistinguishable from each other. Källenius described the design of the latest GLA as “clearly electric-first,” so it’s perhaps appropriate that the EV version is the first one we’re driving.

Sources indicate that electric-first is also the go-to-market strategy—at least in Europe. It was to be in the U.S., too, but there’s been a reversal; we’re now slated to get the GLA hybrid first. Really, though, we won’t be getting either one for a while. We’re told to expect the gas-engine GLA sometime late next year, while the EV won’t arrive until the first half of 2028. Our recent drive of the electric GLA in Spain, therefore, was an extra-long-lead preview.

See all results for upcoming 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA-Class EV for sale near 85705.

In a recent development, we’d say that gives buyers plenty of time to warm up to the newly introduced styling, except that the look is not all that different from the current GLA. More substantial, maybe: The body is bigger, sitting astride a wheelbase that is stretched 2.4 inches. The new GLA is also longer, lower, and wider.

In a recent development, the GLA EV is also adorned with more three-pointed stars, though not to the extent of some other recent Mercedes products. Besides the illuminated logo on the flat-panel “grille,” there’s a large badge on the rear liftgate, and the motif also appears in the headlights and taillights. Opt for Sky Control for the standard glass roof panel, and 172 light-up stars appear on the glass, which is electronically dimmable in sections.

Recent findings suggest that the dash is lifted straight from the GLA’s sedan sibling, the CLA. As in other Benz models, there’s an available Superscreen that adds a 14.0-inch passenger display to the standard 14.0-inch center touchscreen and 10.3-inch instrument screen. With it, virtually the entire dashboard is given over to digital real estate. Sadly, almost none of the space contains any physical switchgear, although at least we still get air vents that can be aimed by hand. Wireless smartphone mirroring is standard, but a wireless charging pad costs extra. The navigation uses Google Maps and optionally offers Benz’s augmented reality, an inset showing a forward-camera view with overlaid arrows indicating direction. Unfortunately, that inset appears on the left side of the touchscreen, where it’s obscured by the driver’s right hand on the wheel; you have to peer around to see it.

It has been revealed that the on-screen climate controls are another ergonomic fail, as the touch points to change the temperature are tiny, and you have to open the climate menu to adjust the fan speed. You could ask for help from Benz’s digital assistant, which lurks within the screen, always listening. And there’s a camera trained on the driver, which can use facial recognition to automatically call up the driver’s profile and saved preferences. It can also take selfies! In a more worthwhile use of technology, buyers can purchase dash-cam functionality for the forward-facing camera.

See all results for new 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA-Class EV for sale near 85705.

According to recent reports, beyond the digital, the interior features high-back front seats that are firmly padded and well shaped. The high center console makes for a somewhat confining feel up front, but its floating design creates a large open bay underneath for storage. The rear-seat area boasts a flat floor and is much roomier than in the CLA sedan. The cargo hold is 15 cubic feet, expandable to 49 cubes with the rear seatbacks folded. There’s also a frunk that’s about the size of a carry-on suitcase.

Sources indicate that the powertrains mirror the CLA EV’s. There’s a single-motor GLA250+ that sends 268 horsepower to the rear wheels. The dual-motor GLA350 4Matic has all-wheel drive and 349 horses. Both employ a two-speed transmission on the rear axle for improved efficiency at highway speeds.

Recent findings suggest that the standard suspension has passive dampers, but the cars we drove had the optional adaptive dampers and rode on 20-inch wheels (18s are standard; 19s are also available). The smooth pavement of Barcelona and sunny coastal environs gave the dampers little to adapt to—any real assessment of the GLA’s ride quality will have to wait until we drive one on the meaner streets back home. However, the suspension acquitted itself well on our drive route’s long series of hillside curves. The GLA is composed but would be more confidence-inspiring if the steering weren’t so light and remote.

Sources indicate that the GLA isn’t a hot hatch, though; it’s more of an urban runabout. In that context, the 268-hp GLA250+ is adequately peppy, even though Mercedes posits a rather languid 60-mph time of 7.2 seconds. We expect it to do better than that, as the CLA250+ we tested managed a 5.8-second result. The dual-motor GLA350 felt much more energetic, particularly outside of urban environs, where it swiftly passed dawdlers on two-lane roads and merged easily onto the freeway. For the GLA350, Mercedes claims a 5.3-second 60-mph time, but again that’s likely an undersell; testing a mechanically identical CLA350, we got 4.3 seconds. Even so, there are quicker EVs in this class, but one positive here is that even the higher-horsepower dual-motor version doesn’t feel like its output overwhelms its chassis—often an issue with high-horsepower EVs. Besides the standard drive modes of Eco, Comfort, Sport, and Individual, the dual-motor GLA adds a Terrain mode that optimizes the powertrain for loose surfaces; its camera system is able to stitch together a “transparent hood” view of what’s immediately in front of the car.

It has been revealed that when it comes time for slowing, there are three levels of liftoff regen (D, D+, and D-), as well as an Auto setting that varies the regen level based on info from the navigation system and the forward-facing cameras. Our preference is D-, which is essentially coasting, but D+ will please fans of one-pedal driving. We also tried the automated parking function, which was able to back into and out of a parallel-parking spot without trying our patience. It’s a digital add-on that’s purchased for a set time period; the same goes for the MBUX Entertainment package of multimedia streaming and app downloads.

Recent findings suggest that like the CLA EV sedan, the GLA is built on Benz’s MMA platform, with an 800-volt architecture and an 85-kWh battery. That architecture allows for speedy DC recharging, up to 320 kilowatts. Should you find a power source robust enough to reach that figure, Mercedes states the GLA battery can go from 10 percent to 80 percent in 22 minutes. (In our testing of the CLA250+ with the same hardware, it went from 10 to 80 percent in just 21 minutes.) EPA range estimates for the GLA aren’t yet available, but the CLA offers a clue, and its impressive range figures run from 312 miles on the low end to as high as 374 miles.

According to recent reports, if the GLA ends up with numbers like those, it’ll look pretty good against the electric Mini Countryman, Genesis GV60, and Cadillac Optiq, and similar-ish to a Rivian R2. Those look to be the GLA EV’s prime competitors at a base-price guesstimate of around $50K. But the EV landscape could shift significantly by the time the GLA gets here. After all, a lot can happen between now and 2028.

#155679. The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (926 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.
  • Industry observers note that spend enough time browsing upcoming e-bike launches and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power.
  • If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.

These days, apparently those are rookie numbers.

Industry observers note that spend enough time browsing upcoming e-bike launches and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power. Dual-motor models have turned the spec sheet into an arms race, with manufacturers seemingly competing to see who can slap the biggest number onto the product page.

If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.

To be clear, I’m not anti-power. I’ve ridden everything from dainty 250W European commuter bikes to electric motorcycles with enough power to rearrange your chest cavity. Powerful electric two-wheelers are fun, period.

But there’s a difference between building a powerful electric two-wheeler and pretending that every powerful electric two-wheeler is still an electric bicycle.

In the US, the widely adopted three-class e-bike system generally tops out at 20 mph (32 km/h) for Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes and 28 mph (45 km/h) for Class 3, with some minor exceptions, and 750 watts has long been a common benchmark for the motor power limit.

Yet browse online e-bike retailers today and you’ll find plenty of machines advertised with motors well beyond that figure, often capable of speeds far beyond normal electric bicycle classifications.

Sometimes there’s a disclaimer explaining that the bike is intended for “off-road use.” Sometimes there’s a software setting that supposedly limits it for street riding.

And sometimes people just sort of squint at the pedals and agree to keep calling it an electric bicycle.

Recent findings suggest that the problem isn’t that 2,000W electric two-wheelers exist. I love lightweight electric motorcycles and mopeds, or what some are beginning to refer to as ‘e-motos’, despite that terminology having its own challenges. So sure, those bikes are great and there is a time and place for such power. The problem is that the industry increasingly seems afraid to call them what they are.

Part of the blame belongs to consumers – to us.

Industry observers note that E-bike shopping has become increasingly spec-sheet driven, and wattage provides an incredibly easy number to compare. If ‘Bike A’ has a 750W motor and ‘Bike B’ costs the same but advertises 1,500W, it’s easy to assume ‘Bike B’ is twice as good. This is especially true for younger riders who lack a deeper understanding of how e-bikes work, and just want something powerful and fast to impress their friends after school. They beg their parents for the latest models with the biggest motors, and many parents give in.

The problem is that’s not how electric bikes work – there’s so much more to a bike than the motor wattage rating.

It has been revealed that motor design, controller current, battery voltage, thermal management, gearing, efficiency and software tuning all influence performance. A beautifully tuned 500W or 750W system can be far nicer to ride – and sometimes more useful – than a poorly implemented motor advertising twice the power.

But “excellent controller tuning” doesn’t look nearly as exciting in a giant font on an Amazon listing. So manufacturers respond rationally based on what consumers demand: They make the number bigger.

The result is an e-bike horsepower war that is ultimately hurting the entire industry.

It has been revealed that when riders blast through bike paths on motorcycle-performance machines marketed as “e-bikes,” pedestrians don’t care whether the motor technically arrived in a street-legal mode. Police officers aren’t going to inspect controller settings. And lawmakers aren’t famous for approaching emerging transportation technology with surgical precision.

They see a fast machine with pedals, hear complaints about dangerous “e-bikes,” and start writing laws that affect everyone – including riders on perfectly ordinary commuter e-bikes.

In my opinion, that’s the part that should worry anyone who enjoys riding an e-bike.

What we have is that essentially all of these things are mopeds (i.e. Class 3 at 40km/h) and not much like bicycles at all.

It isn't surprising that allowing people to ride around unregistered mopeds, often on infrastructure shared with pedestrians, has created a lot of strife.

Quite a lot of them are actually even more extreme than that, and really more like 125cc motorbikes.

In a recent development, there’s absolutely a place for high-powered electric two-wheelers. In fact, I want more of them. Lightweight electric mopeds and motorcycles could replace an enormous number of car trips while using a fraction of the energy and space. Those are highly capable machines, but they need to be used appropriately, registered legally, and ridden responsibly.

And we don’t help that cause by pretending they’re bicycles.

Perhaps the e-bike industry’s next great innovation doesn’t need another 500 watts.

Recent findings suggest that maybe it just needs a little more honesty about what we’re actually building. So let’s build more electric bicycles. And yes, let’s build more e-motos and electric motorcycles. But let’s not confuse the two, either.

#155678. High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Shows

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1280 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Shows

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a upcoming study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.
  • The researchers from Arizona State University said a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.
  • The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a upcoming study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.

The researchers from Arizona State University said a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.

The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.

The researchers published their findings on November 12 in the journal Stem Cell Reports.

The researchers mentioned the study is key because 1 in 25 people develop colon cancer in their lifetime. In the United States, that translates into about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer every year. About 55,000 males and 55,000 females are expected to die from the disease in 2026.

Experts not involved in the study say the research provides valuable information, but they have reservations about the results, as the findings do not yet apply to humans.

“The findings provide a potential mechanism linking diet to intestinal cancer development, but we need to be cautious about translating these results to humans,” remarked Dalia Perelman, MS, CDE, a research dietitian at Stanford University in California.

In a recent development, “We already have evidence from human studies that obesity and certain dietary patterns, particularly those high in processed meats and low in fiber-rich foods, are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk,” Perelman told Healthline. “This study adds a potentially key mechanism to investigate, but it does not establish that dietary fat itself increases colorectal cancer risk in humans.”.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, shared similar views.

“This study provides a better understanding at the cellular level of how a high fat diet may contribute to colorectal cancer development,” Thanki told Healthline.

“Animal studies are an notable starting point for understanding biological processes, but we must be cautious about directly applying their findings to humans,” he added. “Mice and humans share many cellular and biological mechanisms, which makes these studies valuable in identifying potential pathways involved in disease development. However, human diets, genetics, metabolism, and environmental exposures are more complex.”.

To reach their findings, the Arizona State researchers fed mice what the scientists described as a Western-style high fat diet for 6 months.

They then compared those results with those from mice given a low fat diet.

According to recent reports, the researchers remarked the mice on the high fat diet gained more weight than the mice on the low-fat diet. They also developed more intestinal stem cells, and those cells grew at a more rapid rate.

They added that mice genetically predisposed to intestinal cancer who were fed a high-fat diet developed more and larger tumors.

The researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may help explain their increased growth and survival.

They also pointed out that stem cell behavior returned to normal after high fat diet mice were switched to a low fat diet, although some DNA changes persisted. After four weeks, approximately 18% of these changes remained.

When mice were returned to a high fat diet, the researchers stated their intestinal stem cells responded more promptly and strongly than those of mice exposed to the diet for the first time.

They concluded that the study suggests that maintaining a healthy, low fat diet may help regulate intestinal stem cell growth and reduce colon cancer risk.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, RD, president of KAK Consulting and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Ohio, wasn’t involved in the study but highlighted a particular aspect of the findings.

It has been revealed that “What I found particularly interesting was that even after the mice returned to a low fat diet, some of the molecular changes persisted,” she told Healthline. “This raises questions about how our dietary patterns over time may influence long-term health.”.

Experts said these fresh findings are interesting but noted numerous caveats.

It has been revealed that “One important takeaway is that dietary habits over time matter,” remarked Thanki. “Even if someone has consumed a high fat diet for years, making changes now may still provide meaningful health benefits.”.

“I also think these findings are particularly important for children and adolescents, as establishing healthier dietary habits early in life may provide long-term benefits,” he added.

According to recent reports, however, Thanki noted that not all fats are the same. “The health risks depend partly on the type of fat consumed, how much is consumed, and what foods make up the overall diet,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that “Diets consistently high in saturated fats, particularly those containing large amounts of processed meats, fried foods, and highly processed products, can contribute to obesity, elevated cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction. These factors can also contribute to chronic inflammation and may increase the risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer,” Thanki continued.

Perelman said the diet used in the study was extremely high in fat, providing 60% of calories from fat, primarily from lard.

“We know that the health effects of dietary fats differ depending on their sources and fatty acid composition, and we cannot assume that a diet rich in unsaturated fats from foods such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds would produce the same effects,” she noted.

Perelman added that the researchers primarily studied stem cells from the small intestine rather than the colon.

“Although these tissues share some biological characteristics, they have important differences, and we cannot assume that the same changes would occur in the colon,” she explained.

Finally, Perelman noted that “the mice consuming the high fat diet also gained weight, making it difficult to separate the effects of dietary fat itself from those associated with increased body fat and other metabolic changes.”.

Not all high fat foods are unhealthy. Some high fat foods that offer healthy benefits include:.

“The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to eliminate fat because our bodies need healthy fats for normal functioning,” said Thanki. “Instead, people should focus on reducing saturated and trans fats while incorporating healthier unsaturated fats in appropriate amounts.”.

Thanki had several dietary suggestions. Among them:.

Recent findings suggest that “Consistency matters more than perfection. Even modest dietary changes, maintained over time, can have meaningful health benefits,” Thanki remarked.

According to recent reports, perelman agreed. “The overall quality of the diet matters. Diets that are very high in fat may displace other foods and nutrients that have crucial health benefits,” she remarked.

“For colorectal cancer specifically, higher intakes of dietary fiber and whole grains have consistently been associated with lower risk,” Perelman noted.

“Therefore, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing fat, it is important to consider the overall dietary pattern and whether it provides adequate amounts of fiber-rich plant foods and other beneficial nutrients.”.

According to recent reports, kirkpatrick agreed that the type of fat is what is important. “A Mediterranean-style diet that includes olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish can be relatively high in fat but is consistently associated with positive health outcomes,” she said.

“On the other hand, a diet high in saturated fat, processed meats, and ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of certain chronic diseases, particularly when it’s also low in fiber and other protective nutrients.”.

Kirkpatrick also noted that many lifestyle habits contribute to a person’s overall health.

“Our health is influenced by so many factors beyond diet, including how we manage stress, our sleep habits, physical activity, genetics, and overall lifestyle,” she said.

#155677. Industry News: Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (968 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • That brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter.
  • Sources indicate that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere. While the humans fire up their furnaces (or, ideally, heat pumps), animals prepare in their own ways.

That brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter. Most of us were taught things that, over time, were proven to be untrue, and winter behaviors are no exception. Bears, for example, don’t sleep the entire winter. Birds don’t actually care about the cold that much, and migrate for other reasons. And squirrels aren’t constantly forgetting the location of their nuts. Let’s dig into these common winter myths, and what actual research points to.

Sources indicate that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter. It’s not true—bears don’t hibernate. At least, not exactly.

An explainer published by the National Park Service states that hibernation isn’t a black-and-white concept: “In recent years the view that the state of hibernation exists on a spectrum rather than as a binary yes-or-no condition is becoming more entrenched.” The piece goes on to say that black bears don’t hibernate as deeply as smaller animals.

In a recent development, there’s real research backing this up. A 2011 study published in Science by researchers at the University of Alaska Fairbanks reveals that bears get up and shift position throughout the winter. “Animals changed position twice a day to once every 2 days, when they stood, occasionally groomed, and rearranged bedding material,” the study states. The research also states that bears use a great deal more energy during the winter than smaller animals. “During torpor, metabolic rates of small hibernators decrease to 2 to 5 percent of basal metabolic rate (BMR),” the study explains, before showing that bears’ metabolic rates reach closer to 25 percent. That’s a wide spectrum.

Recent findings suggest that so bears don’t sleep all winter—they regularly get up. That brings us to another myth: The idea that bears give birth without waking up. It’s also not true, according to the National Park Service.

Industry observers note that “They’re not only awake during this time, but in the days before birthing, expectant mothers will often add bedding to the den by chewing materials into smaller pieces and arranging them just-so,” the explainer states. “After the 1 to 3 half-ounce to 1 lb cubs are born, she meticulously licks them clean, and provides warmth and mother’s milk as they grow to about 5 lbs by the time they emerge in spring.”.

Which isn’t to say that bears are active in winter—they really do slow down. But they don’t hibernate to the same extent as smaller animals.

According to recent reports, you might think that birds fly south for the winter because they don’t want to freeze—we even call cold-hating humans who travel in winter “snowbirds,” in reference to this belief. But it turns out birds aren’t directly concerned with cold weather.

If you have a bird feeder you’ve probably noticed that many birds stick around for the winter.An explainer by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology states that birds are perfectly capable of surviving winter temperatures. “Escaping cold temperatures is not itself a major factor that drives birds to migrate, since many species, even hummingbirds, can withstand freezing temperatures as long as an adequate supply of food is available,” the article states.

It has been revealed that there’s less food around in the winter, and that’s the actual reason for migration. You might say this is semantics, and you’re not entirely wrong—the cold temperature causes the food shortage. But if you’re picturing shivering birds, desperate to travel somewhere warmer, you’re imagining the wrong motivation. Birds don’t leave in pursuit of warmer weather; they leave in pursuit of food and longer daylight hours. And they head back north (or south) in the spring for the same reason: the thaw means a lot of fresh food, not to mention safe, open areas for breeding.

Squirrels spend a good part of the year hiding nuts, all so they can recover them in the winter. A common legend goes something like this: squirrels forget about most of these nuts, and that’s how forests grow. And while it is true that squirrel caches can become trees, squirrels don’t forget their nuts that often.

Recent findings suggest that they are, in fact, really good at keeping track of their nuts, and this has been known for decades. A 1991 paper published in Animal Behaviour by researchers at Princeton University highlighted this. In the study, captive grey squirrels were all given hazelnuts to bury in the same area. The nuts were then all removed by experimenters. The squirrels were re-introduced to the site, one by one, with a twist: experimenters buried fresh nuts in the squirrel’s own 10 cache sites and an equal number of sites randomly chosen from caches made by other squirrels.

It has been revealed that the results were striking. “Although each squirrel’s own caches were close to the caches of other squirrels, the squirrels retrieved significantly more nuts from their own sites than from sites used by other squirrels, after all delays,” the paper states. “The retrieval accuracy of the squirrels under these conditions indicates that while grey squirrels can locate buried nuts by their odour, they can also remember the individual locations of nuts they have buried.”.

According to recent reports, other studies show how well squirrels can remember nuts. A 2023 study published in Urban Ecosystems by researchers from Poland found that hazelnuts cached by squirrels are more likely to be dug up than hazelnuts buried by humans in the same area. This suggests that squirrels are pretty good at remembering where they buried their nuts.

#155675. Why You’re Stressed When Everyone Else Seems Fine

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (804 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Why You’re Stressed When Everyone Else Seems Fine

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You slam the laptop shut, fighting the urge to scream profanities into the void.
  • According to recent reports, later that day, you remember how calmly your friend reacted when their computer died; they lost not only work but personal photos, videos, and much more.
  • Or, according to an acquaintance of mine, pretty much every day at the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

You type your password carefully.

Maybe the third time is the charm.

Now your account is locked for 24 hours!

You slam the laptop shut, fighting the urge to scream profanities into the void.

According to recent reports, later that day, you remember how calmly your friend reacted when their computer died; they lost not only work but personal photos, videos, and much more. How could something so small stress one person out while something more serious barely affects another? For some people, a messy home is stressful. For others, waiting in line at the bank, being around screaming kids, or Christmas shopping. Stress depends not only on what happens, but on what we think it means, and whether we believe we have the resources to deal with it.

Or, according to an acquaintance of mine, pretty much every day at the office.

Industry observers note that lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model suggests that our different reactions to stressors may come down to primary and secondary appraisal. Primary appraisal involves assessing whether an event matters to us and whether it represents harm, loss, threat, or challenge. Secondary appraisal involves assessing whether we have the resources and options to cope with it. An event can threaten anything that matters to us, be it our health, self-esteem, values, commitments, or goals.

The situation itself influences the appraisal process: how we interpret it, and the resources we believe we have.

According to recent reports, the situation itself: Two people might react very differently to the same situation, yet a closer look shows they aren't really in the same situation. Consider romantic breakups. One person may move on quickly, while another may struggle with the emotional consequences for years. What makes some breakups more stressful than others?

Research suggests that events tend to be more stressful when they are sudden, severe, ambiguous, uncontrollable, or long-lasting. For instance, a sudden, unexpected breakup may be different from a mutual breakup that follows a gradual deterioration in the relationship.

Recent findings suggest that our individual characteristics also influence how we perceive and interpret an event. Namely, personality factors such as higher levels of neuroticism and greater intolerance of uncertainty have been associated with greater stress and distress.

Our values, commitments, and goals also shape how we interpret an event.

Someone who has always imagined a future of marriage and children might experience a potential breakup as a threat not only to their immediate relationship needs, but also to their future and their sense of self. Another person whose identity and goals are strongly focused on career advancement might experience the breakup differently.

According to recent reports, there are different types of resources. Internal resources include skills, experience, physical and mental health, and a sense of agency and control. External resources include practical assistance, social support, money, access to information, and professional help.

It has been revealed that what matters for stress is not just whether these resources exist, but whether we perceive them as available and sufficient to help us cope. For example, someone may have supportive friends or family but not feel comfortable confiding in them (or assume they can't help much). Our appraisal of available resources can influence how threatening or manageable an event feels.

Therefore, a breakup may be more challenging for someone who is socially isolated, dealing with financial difficulties, has limited access to mental health services, or lacks confidence in their ability to cope effectively.

The next time you're wondering why something is stressing you, ask yourself three questions:.

Consider event characteristics, such as suddenness, severity, uncertainty, controllability, and duration.

In a recent development, some threats may be obvious, such as those involving your safety, health, or finances. But a situation can also threaten your goals, values, self-esteem, relationships, or sense of identity.

Industry observers note that 3. Do I believe I can handle it?

Your confidence in your ability to handle it matters; internal and external resources can influence this, including experience, knowledge, social support, health, practical resources, perceived control, and coping skills.

Industry observers note that one final point: comparing your stress response with someone else's can be misleading. We can observe how other people react to events, but we cannot know exactly how they perceive or interpret those events. Just because you experienced more stress than someone else does not mean you are less resilient.

In a recent development, resilience is not the same as stress reactivity. It is about adapting successfully to adversity, not about feeling stress in the first place. A strong stress response is not a judgment on your character. It just says what happened really mattered to you.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX are working toward a year-end deadline to agree on their all-stock merger, according to the Financial Times. A signed deal by December 31 would land days before the upcoming Congress, where Democrats have promised to dig into Musk’s companies, is sworn in on January 3.

Sources indicate that the FT also named the directors negotiating for each side. Two of Tesla’s three are the same people who designed Musk’s $1 trillion pay package.

We’ve been tracking the Tesla-SpaceX merger since Musk first floated it in May, when we called it Musk’s fourth billion-dollar self-deal, and his first trillion-dollar self-deal. Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX could announce the deal as soon as December. The FT report adds a deadline, names and a vote threshold.

According to the FT, the talks are “moving towards a potential year-end deadline,” even though people familiar with the negotiations say an agreement isn’t close. The combined group would be worth about $3.5 trillion, by far the largest merger ever.

It has been revealed that so why year-end? Look at the calendar.

Sources indicate that the new Congress is seated on January 3. As of November 24, AP’s count has Democrats at 258 House seats and 56 Senate seats. Democrats haven’t been subtle about what comes next: Sen. Ruben Gallego tagged Musk on X with “See you in January,” and SpaceX’s military contracts and Musk’s Starlink decisions over Ukraine are expected to be early investigation targets.

It’s not only Washington. Texas’ incoming attorney general told Bloomberg that a merger of this size “warrants tremendous scrutiny,” and Bloomberg had previously reported that the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

Recent findings suggest that tesla’s special committee is chair Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung, advised by Evercore. SpaceX is represented by Roelof Botha and Randy Glein, with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs as advisers. Both banks also helped take SpaceX public in June.

Sources indicate that denholm and Wilson-Thompson should sound familiar. They were the two-person special committee that built Musk’s upcoming CEO pay package after a Delaware judge voided his 2018 award. And that 2025 award has change-in-control terms that drop its operational milestones and vest earned shares at the deal price, so the committee that wrote it is now negotiating the deal that could trigger it.

Ira Ehrenpreis, a long-time friend of Musk, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees and has sat on SpaceX’s board since February, isn’t on Tesla’s committee, per the FT.

In a recent development, if you can believe it, Musk isn’t formally in the room. The FT says Texas governance rules keep him out of active negotiations, but both committees can consult senior executives for information. Every one of those executives reports to Musk.

Recent findings suggest that any agreement goes to a separate extraordinary Tesla shareholder meeting, and it needs more than 50% of all outstanding votes, not just of votes cast. Abstentions and uncast shares effectively count as “no.”.

Industry observers note that that sounds like a high bar. But Musk holds about 20% of Tesla’s voting power, and nothing in the report states his shares will be excluded. If they count, he’s 40% of the way to approval before a single other shareholder votes. On the other side, Musk controls about 84% of SpaceX’s votes, so there’s no real suspense there.

Uncast retail votes are exactly what Tesla’s newly introduced auto-vote program, rolled out in its October proxy, was designed to reduce.

Sources indicate that then there’s the regulatory side. The FT says the deal could draw scrutiny in the US, China, Europe and the UK, with Tesla’s China operations sitting awkwardly next to SpaceX’s rocket and Starlink business, which does a lot of work for the US military. Giga Shanghai builds more than half of Tesla’s cars.

Congress can’t block this merger. Antitrust review sits with Trump’s DOJ and FTC until 2029, plus China, the EU and the UK.

Recent findings suggest that it's probably already too late to escape Jan 3. The DoJ investigation into the merger will take a minimum of a few months. At the very least it looks like there is a 30 mandatory waiting period, so if the merger isn't revealed by Dec 4, that 30 days takes them to Jan 3. That gives them 10 calendar days to finish negotiations and get stock holder approval and they have to give time for the voters to get their votes in. So short of some miracle, Musk isn't going to get this done before Jan 3 ... at least from my understanding and counting.

What congressional committees can do is subpoena. Committee minutes, the Evercore fairness work, emails between Denholm’s committee and Musk’s executives about how the exchange ratio got set. That’s the kind of record that got Musk’s 2018 pay package voided by a Delaware judge, and it’s the kind of record nobody wants dragged into a hearing mid-negotiation.

In a recent development, the talks are “not close,” yet there’s a deadline. When the deadline comes from the political calendar instead of the negotiation, the side that wants to close fast is the one giving ground. But in this case, Musk is both sides, but he is mainly SpaceX.

We’ve noted it before, and we’ll keep saying it: the only vote that means anything here is a majority of Tesla shareholders not named Musk. Denholm, who is up for re-election at next week’s December 3 annual meeting, could commit to that today, but in her entire tenure as Tesla chair, she always did exactly what Musk wanted.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, this could be a great way to meet the demands of more people. Designers love a clean dashboard without physical buttons and switches. Plenty of drivers really love having that switchgear. This system allows owners to pick whatever they want on the fly.

The timing makes plenty of sense too. Audi has openly remarked that it views moving toward more mechanical controls as the right direction. Of course, adding extra complexity to the once-simple idea of buttons also can increase the cost down the line when it comes time for repairs, but even so, this idea is certainly a fascinating solution to a very modern problem.

#155671. Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (823 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown.
  • That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study.
  • It has been revealed that using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench indicates they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

It has been revealed that using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”.

“Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, said in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”.

Industry observers note that reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

The robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that  hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

It has been revealed that in this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”.

According to recent reports, the unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well:  the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

#155669. The Emotion Nobody Mentions When We Talk About Money

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1487 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Emotion Nobody Mentions When We Talk About Money

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • It has been revealed that when Anna felt low, she went shopping.
  • It faded almost as soon as she left, and by the time the credit card bill arrived, shame and regret had taken its place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

It has been revealed that when Anna felt low, she went shopping. Anna is a social worker I interviewed while researching financial well-being, and she told me about a particular kind of shop she was drawn to: soft fabrics, quiet music, a faint scent of something expensive. Her home and her workplace were busy and chaotic. In the shop, nothing bad could happen. Her biggest decision was which color coat to choose for spring.

The calm never lasted. It faded almost as soon as she left, and by the time the credit card bill arrived, shame and regret had taken its place.

Today is Black Friday, a day built on the promise that the right purchase will make us feel better. For many of us, as for Anna, the feeling we are trying to shop away is shame.

It is also a feeling we rarely admit to. In a 2025 Bankrate survey, 61% of U.S. adults remarked they were uncomfortable discussing their bank balance. Fewer felt that way about their love life (51%), their political views (24%), or their religion (18%).

Sources indicate that psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett (2017) argues that emotions are constructed by the brain rather than simply triggered. I find it helpful to think of the brain as a weather forecaster. Drawing on past experience, it constantly predicts what our bodily sensations mean, and it revises the forecast as new information comes in.

A knot in your stomach before a job interview could be hunger, dread, or excitement. Which one you feel depends partly on how your brain has learned to read situations like this one.

Recent findings suggest that many of us have years of money forecasts shaped by tension and secrecy at home. Opening a bill or splitting a restaurant check can call up an old forecast before we have even looked at the numbers. Often, that forecast is for shame.

Internal shame is the voice that claims, “I’m bad with money.” It treats missing financial skills as a personal flaw, and a rare one. Everyone else seems to manage. If I struggle, it must say something about who I am.

According to recent reports, this belief often starts early. Many of the middle-aged adults I meet, particularly women, tell me nobody talked openly about money with them when they were growing up. They learned through costly mistakes, and each mistake seemed to confirm that something was wrong with them.

External shame is about how others see us. In 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that the ancient Greeks and Romans lived comfortably without linen, yet in his own day, a respectable laborer would be ashamed to appear in public without a linen shirt. What counts as a necessity depends partly on what we need to avoid being looked down on.

Swedish researcher Bengt Starrin and colleagues (2009) tested this idea in a survey of more than 5,600 adults. Both financial stress and experiences of being shamed predicted psychosocial ill-health, and people who reported both were the most affected. Having too little money is hard, and feeling diminished because of it adds to the harm.

Money shame is not limited to poverty. It can be strongest when, by all appearances, there should be enough.

According to recent reports, ann-Marie is a journalist with three books to her name and steady work for well-known magazines. She is a single mother of two, widowed when her daughters were small. She still pays a large mortgage on a country house she has been unable to sell, while renting in the city near her daughters’ music schools. Her income is reasonable, but she has no buffer. One unexpected bill sets her back, and she knows what it means to stretch her last ten euros across a week of groceries.

According to recent reports, she skips most social events because they cost money. She never mentions her worries to her daughters, which makes it hard to explain why they rarely travel or why her laptop comes along on weekends. To others, her life looks successful. She keeps the rest to herself.

Industry observers note that ann-Marie is far from alone. In the American Psychological Association’s Stress in America 2023 survey, 82% of adults aged 18 to 34 named money as a significant source of stress.

In a recent development, shame is a social emotion. It probably evolved to keep us in good standing with our group, but when it takes hold, it does undeniable damage. A meta-analysis of 108 studies found that shame is more strongly linked to depressive symptoms than guilt is (Kim et al., 2011).

According to recent reports, with money, shame can also make the original problem worse. Joe Gladstone and colleagues (2021) studied this using bank records, longitudinal surveys, and comparisons of identical twins. Across six studies, people who felt financial shame were more likely to disengage from their finances. That disengagement led to poorer financial decisions, which deepened their hardship. The researchers call this a financial shame spiral, something many of us are familiar with in our daily lives.

Fear of judgment adds to the feeling of shame. In a study of middle-class consumers in debt, those who expected to be stigmatized hid their debt from friends and family, put off seeking help, and even spent more in social situations to keep up appearances (Moorhouse et al., 2023).

Sources indicate that it’s a bit like a leak you are too embarrassed to report. The longer you hide it, the more damage it does to the house.

It has been revealed that the shame researcher Brené Brown (2007) describes empathy as the antidote to shame. Here are some ways to put that into practice with money.

Start with understanding rather than resolutions. Vowing to take control and cut out every bad habit rarely lasts. It helps more to ask how you got here. What did you learn about money as a child? What might your spending or avoidance have been protecting you from?

Name the feeling. When a money task makes you tense, try saying to yourself, “This is shame.” Brain-imaging research reveals that putting feelings into words reduces activity in the amygdala, a region involved in emotional alarm (Lieberman et al., 2007). Naming the feeling may give your forecast a chance to patch.

According to recent reports, remember that financial skills are learned. If you never learned them, that reflects what you were taught, and indicates nothing about your character. In Gladstone’s research, an intervention built around affirming acts of kindness weakened the link between shame and disengagement.

Recent findings suggest that talk to someone. In a field experiment, people who took a financial course alongside others in the same situation paid off more debt than people in the control group. Among those most afraid of judgment, learning in a group also improved well-being more than learning privately did (Moorhouse et al., 2023). A friend, a partner, or a financial counselor can all be a starting point.

For Anna, the work was learning to find calm without a new purchase. Part of that was looking a little further ahead and asking what feeling each shopping trip would leave behind. That question is worth asking today, before checkout.

#155668. Nuro pulls safety drivers from Lucid Gravity Uber robotaxis in Bay Area

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (890 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Nuro pulls safety drivers from Lucid Gravity Uber robotaxis in Bay Area

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nuro is now testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with nobody in the driver’s seat.
  • Industry observers note that it’s the biggest step yet for the Uber-Nuro-Lucid partnership.
  • Industry observers note that according to Nuro’s announcement, driverless testing covers Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, with more Bay Area cities to follow next year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nuro is now testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with nobody in the driver’s seat. The driverless testing starts in four Peninsula and South Bay cities, with a fleet of more than 100 Gravity SUVs delivered by Lucid for the program.

Industry observers note that it’s the biggest step yet for the Uber-Nuro-Lucid partnership. But it comes with a quieter update: the public launch, originally promised for 2026, is now expected in Q1 2027.

Industry observers note that according to Nuro’s announcement, driverless testing covers Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, with more Bay Area cities to follow next year. Uber employees will “soon” be able to ride in the driverless vehicles.

Sources indicate that nuro has run the Gravity robotaxis around the clock in the Bay Area and Houston since December 2025, but always with a safety driver. Before pulling the driver, the firm indicates it ran no-vehicle-operator testing at its Las Vegas closed course, covering things like pedestrian encounters and right-of-way violations, plus large-scale simulation.

Recent findings suggest that tilo Schwarz, Nuro’s head of the Nuro Driver, pointed out that driverless operation “isn’t newly introduced” for the organization. That’s fair. Nuro has run driverless delivery pods in California since 2020. But this is its first time doing it with a passenger vehicle.

Sources indicate that the regulatory pieces were already in place. As we reported in May, the California DMV extended Nuro’s driverless testing permit to the Lucid Gravity, and the CPUC followed with a drivered pilot permit for carrying passengers.

In a recent development, nuro states it’s one of just six companies allowed to test without a driver on California roads. The DMV’s list, last updated November 5, confirms it: AutoMo, Nuro, Tensor, Waymo, WeRide, and Zoox.

Tesla isn’t one of them. Its “Tesla Robotaxi LLC” entity only holds a permit to test with a driver in California, and it has no deployment permit either.

Industry observers note that waymo, of course, is the benchmark. It already runs a paid, fully driverless service across much of the Bay Area, including the Peninsula and South Bay where Nuro is just now pulling its safety drivers.

According to recent reports, when Lucid, Nuro, and Uber unveiled the program in July 2025, the plan was to launch “later next year” in a major US city. As recently as June, when Uber named Houston as the second market for mid-2027, the Bay Area launch was still slated for this year.

Now it’s Q1 2027. Not a huge slip, but it’s a slip.

In a recent development, the scale ambition has gone the other way. Uber’s purchase commitment grew from 20,000 vehicles to at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles with the Nuro Driver, starting with the Gravity and later Lucid’s upcoming midsize models. Uber will own and operate the cars with fleet partners, and they’ll only be available through the Uber app.

For context, Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3 2026. At that pace, 35,000 robotaxis would take more than two years of Lucid’s entire output.

Recent findings suggest that this is real progress, and it deserves credit. Nuro got the permits, built a formal safety case, tested at a closed course, and only then took the driver out. That’s how it should be done, and it should be applauded, especially as some companies claim to lead in autonomy while being too chicken to get a permit in California.

In a recent development, but let’s keep it in perspective. Driverless testing in four suburban cities with a 100-car fleet is where Waymo was years ago. Waymo is already doing hundreds of thousands of paid rides a week, including in the same part of the Bay Area. Nuro and Uber aren’t catching up to Waymo in 2027.

The bigger question for me is Lucid. The partnership gives Lucid exactly the kind of volume it needs, and 35,000 vehicles is a big number for a tech giant delivering under 4,000 cars a quarter.

If this program is successful, and that’s a big if, then it could really help Lucid get to its more affordable vehicle.

#155665. Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (536 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe.
  • Sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE.
  • “The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals new insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich mentioned in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe. This physical and cultural separation seems to have existed for a very long time. Archaeological evidence on either side of the river as early as the late fourth millennia BCE reveals differences. Archaeologists have determined that the river is a sort of barrier during this time—but new research challenges this conclusion.

Sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. His findings, described in a study recently published in the archaeological journal Germania, suggest that populations in Western, Central, and Northern Europe were more connected than previously assumed.

“The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals new insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich mentioned in a statement.

The pottery in question, called coarse ware, is simple and plain—so much so that archaeologists have seen it as culturally insignificant. The roughly-shaped artifacts have emerged in many regions of Europe. It became widespread in modern-day central and northern France as well as the western Alpine region starting in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Afterward, it also became prominent in modern-day western and northern Germany and Denmark.

It has been revealed that “There are indications that a convergence of pottery styles across such great distances occurred gradually and unconsciously. This is an indicator of high mobility within a region where there were no distinct barriers between groups, or where the boundaries were fluid,” said Schultrich.

Double stone axes—prestigious axes with two cutting edges and a shaft hole—were also widespread in this period. Archaeologists have discovered them from France through Central Europe to Scandinavia and Poland. While the dates of the French double stone axes has been a subject of contention, it’s right now clear that they, along with the Central and Northern European versions, hail from the the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. Unlike coarse ware, the double axe design seems to have been intentionally widespread, showing that a shared concept existed on either side of the river.

Recent findings suggest that the same regions are also home to different versions of large-scale group burials, including passage graves or gallery graves. But they all were the final resting place of dozens to hundreds of individuals, were used over many generations, and were the locations of ritual acts and gatherings. This is more evidence of a shared idea, even though its regional manifestation differed.

Recent findings suggest that “It was not a uniform cultural complex,” Schultrich explained. “What we see here is a network characterised by fundamental narratives, yet one that simultaneously allowed scope for strong regional peculiarities. This is an early example of a complex, differentiated form of society in which identity combined both supra-regional and local elements.”.

By drawing prehistoric connections across the Rhine, Schultrich revealed ties across late Neolithic Europe that clearly overcame the watery boundary.
