📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD rolled out the third-generation Tang, a large, high-tech five-seat flagship electric SUV, starting at under $30,000 in China.

The new third-gen Tang is positioned below the Great Tang, or “Da Tang” as it’s called in China, BYD’s larger seven-seat flagship SUV in its Dynasty lineup.

In a recent development, BYD held a launch event for its new flagship five-seat electric SUV on Tuesday. The third-gen Tang is available in three variants: standard Premium, Laser Premium, and Laser Flagship.

All versions come standard with rear-wheel drive (RWD), but buyers can upgrade the Laser Flagship model with an optional all-wheel-drive (AWD) steer-by-wire package for an extra 20,000 yuan ($3,000).

Prices for the standard Tang Premium start at 187,900 yuan, or about $28,000, significantly lower than its pre-sale price of 225,000 yuan ($34,000).

The Laser Premium and Laser Flagship models start at 207,900 yuan and 219,900 yuan, respectively, also well below the pre-sale price.

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade LFP Batteries. RWD models use a single 402 hp (300kW) electric motor, delivering CLTC ranges of 453 miles (730 km) for the base Premium model and 528 miles (850 km) for the Laser Premium and Laser Flagship versions.

Upgrading to the dual-motor AWD powertrain bumps power to 690 hp (515 kW) and delivers a CLTC range of up to 478 miles (770 km).

The optional AWD steer-by-wire package adds a premium touch with a drive-by-wire digital chassis, reclining driver’s seats, a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display screen, and intelligent electric all-wheel-drive.

All versions feature BYD’s Flash Charging tech, enabling it to charge from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes for a full recharge (10% to 97%).

Inside, the flagship SUV adopts a five-seat layout and is packed with huge digital screens and premium extras.

The third-gen Tang features two giant screens: a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display and a 30″ panoramic theater screen.

According to recent reports, BYD stated the five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers, claiming the upcoming Tang SUV has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L. It also offers a generous 1,000 mm of legroom for rear passengers.

The flagship electric SUV is equipped with BYD’s latest tech and other features, including its God’s Eye B laser-assisted driving system with DiPilot300 and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

In a recent development, A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season. United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) volunteer and photographer Dan Rapp spotted the egg on George and Geraldine’s nest this weekend. The pair are endangered short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian, and this is their 10th straight year together.

According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.

In a recent development, short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill. The monogamous birds can live up to 50 years, and nest on islands and atolls where they typically lay one egg per season. Short-tailed albatrosses are listed as endangered, and biologists estimate that there are only 10,000 left in the wild.

Industry observers note that george and Geraldine were banded as chicks on Torishima Island, Japan. They raised their first chick together during the 2018–2019 breeding season. The duo is the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, but other members of their species were observed last season. After spending the summer/non-nesting season apart, George was first spotted at Midway Atoll on October 18. He was reunited with Geraldine by October 22.

In a recent development, this remote group of islands sit about 1,250 miles from Hawaii’s capital Honolulu and are most famous for a pivotal World War II battle. Every fall, it becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species. Some notable albatross species are the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species and the Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis). At over 70 years old, a Laysan albatross named Wisdom claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird. She has produced roughly 50 to 60 eggs, and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime, and she became a grandmother once again in March. Wisdom has not been spotted yet this nesting season.

Industry observers note that bird enthusiasts from around the world can eavesdrop on this albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates. Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch fluffy albatross chicks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somehow, after all these years, there are still a considerable number of vehicles equipped with Takata airbags, though their number should be considerably lower in the near future. Honda just issued a recall for 810,592 cars equipped with Takata airbags that could rupture due to propellant degradation caused by high humidity.

According to documents filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the recall covers some 2013 Acura RDX, ILX, Honda CR-V, Civic, and Accord models. The affected Accords and Acuras are all from the 2013 model year, while the CR-V and Civic populations include both 2012 and 2013 vehicles.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94043.

The NHTSA documents show that the affected vehicles are equipped with airbag inflators that use a phase-stabilized ammonium nitrate propellant, which is intended to control moisture within the inflator. Over time, exposure to high humidity and repeated temperature changes can cause the inflator to become brittle. When the brittle inflators are deployed, they could turn into projectiles that shoot metal fragments through the cabin, potentially injuring or killing occupants.

In a recent development, the recall comes after years of investigation and analysis by Honda, which was routinely shared with NHTSA. The recall documents show that on November 19, 2026, Honda determined that the inflators posed enough of a risk to warrant the new recall.

Industry observers note that owners of affected models will be contacted by mail and urged to bring their vehicle to a Honda or Acura dealership. Dealer technicians will replace the driver and passenger airbag inflators with a different model for free. Dealers have already been notified of the recall, with owner notification letters scheduled to be sent on December 18. Owners concerned that their car might be included in the recall can check on the NHTSA recalls site as well as NHTSA’s dedicated Takata airbag recall page.

#155658. Tech Report: What Elizabeth Holmes's Stare Doesn’t Say

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (841 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What Elizabeth Holmes's Stare Doesn’t Say

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary You Can See Everything, the camera cuts to a tight close-up of the upper half of Elizabeth Holmes’s face.
  • Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, has the same wide blue eyes and unblinking gaze.
  • Blinking is a coordinated sensorimotor action that protects the eyes while reflecting shifts in attention and cognitive load.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Recent findings suggest that in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary You Can See Everything, the camera cuts to a tight close-up of the upper half of Elizabeth Holmes’s face. Her large blue eyes hold Fielder’s gaze for an extraordinarily long time without blinking. It was quite distracting. I found myself counting the seconds between blinks and trying to match them. I couldn’t keep up.

Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, has the same wide blue eyes and unblinking gaze. It was unnerving to watch them even in the safety of my own living room.

Blinking is a coordinated sensorimotor action that protects the eyes while reflecting shifts in attention and cognitive load. Adults typically blink about 14 to 17 times per minute, with each blink lasting roughly 100 to 300 milliseconds.

In a recent development, people naturally blink less when they’re working hard to focus. Studies in cognitive and auditory neuroscience show that people systematically blink less during moments of high cognitive demand. For example, people blink less in noisy environments so they don’t miss visual cues like lip movement.

Sources indicate that holmes and Evans don’t just blink less; their wide-eyed look demonstrates white around the iris. This effect comes from how far the eyelids open, not how often they close. Put the two together—wide-open lids and a low blink rate—and you get a jarring laser-focused stare. The iris, an orb floating in a white sea of sclera.

Sources indicate that research by Tamami Nakano found that people watching someone speak tend to sync their blinks with the speaker's. When I tried to match Holmes's blinks and failed, I was consciously doing what viewers do without noticing.

It has been revealed that psychologists Sharon Leal and Aldert Vrij found that people blinked less when they lied and blinked more than usual right afterward. Their 2008 research concluded that lying is cognitively demanding. Blinking slows while the lie is being told, then rebounds once it's over.

Industry observers note that I’m not suggesting Holmes is a liar. Someone who blinks less might be lying, but they may also be concentrating, self-conscious in front of a camera, on medication, or simply a person who blinks less than average. A low blink rate, in and of itself, suggests someone may be working hard. It doesn’t tell us at what.

Holmes’s stare also reminded me of Anthony Hopkins’s Oscar-winning performance as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs. Hopkins said in an interview that he deliberately minimized blinking while playing the cannibalistic serial killer. The result was an unflinching performance that made Lecter feel oddly calm, predatory, and menacing.

It has been revealed that while popular culture associates unblinking stares with sociopathy, the research doesn’t support it. In fact, some studies suggest that people high in psychopathic traits pay less attention to other people’s eyes, not more. An unblinking stare is not a reliable indicator of a personality disorder. It can be an effective tool for an actor or for a young founder delivering a TEDMED talk, as Holmes did in 2014. But it’s not diagnostic.

In the 2005 bestseller Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking, author Malcolm Gladwell argued that snap judgments and first impressions formed within the first two seconds can be just as accurate as slow, deliberate analysis. “There can be as much value in the blink of an eye as in months of rational analysis,” he wrote.

Gladwell wasn’t writing about literal blinking, but he attached a condition that matters here: fast judgments are trustworthy only when they’re grounded in real experience.

Sources indicate that my first reaction to Holmes and Evans was a snap judgment. I don’t have any real expertise in reading blink rates. What I have is a cultural script (Hannibal Lecter, the wide-eyed villain) and an expectation about conversational rhythm, which includes blinking and looking away occasionally.

That doesn’t make my unease any less valid. It was real information about me. It told me that Holmes’s stare had broken a social rhythm, and that I was primed to read that break as menace.

The documentary title promises we can see everything. The close-up on Holmes’s eyes reminds us we can’t. All we can see is that she isn’t blinking. We can’t see why.

#155656. Wasps recognize faces—and it keeps them from killing each other

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (562 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Wasps recognize faces—and it keeps them from killing each other

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that wasps can recognize faces.
  • Industry observers note that “These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” Christopher Jernigan, a study co-author and neuroethologist  at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, noted in a statement.
  • Industry observers note that the team studied the northern paper wasp (Polistes fuscates).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that wasps can recognize faces. But don’t worry. They may not be telling human faces apart the way that cows can. The stingy insects tell their nestmates apart by recognizing different color patterns on their faces, so they know the difference between mama wasp and papa wasp or a friend versus a foe. A study published today in the journal Cell details how they use specialized brain cells to pull this off.

Industry observers note that “These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” Christopher Jernigan, a study co-author and neuroethologist  at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, noted in a statement. “These groups of neurons are all firing, and each neuron has a slightly different preference for one face or another.”.

Industry observers note that the team studied the northern paper wasp (Polistes fuscates). These roughly half-inch long bugs are found from southern parts of Canada through Florida and Texas. Their name comes from the paper-like nests made of hexagonal cells that they often construct under building eaves and on the ceilings of porches. Paper wasps also have silk that shine under UV light, giving these nests a secretive fluorescent glow.

Sources indicate that female northern paper wasps use facial recognition to remember another wasp’s place in the nest’s hierarchy. Once this hierarchy is established, recognizing faces helps maintain social order, without a constant battle for dominance.

Sources indicate that wasps may be using a method for facial recognition that’s similar to how primates (including humans) tell faces apart, even though both methods evolved independently. Even with brains about the size of a single rice grain, Jernigan said that wasps are “able to do this incredibly complex task of remembering and recalling individuals.” They do this by spotting the differences between the color patterns on one wasp face versus another, with the help of specialized neurons.

Recent findings suggest that wasps can also perform something called social eavesdropping. When two wasps fight to establish dominance in the nest hierarchy, one wasps can watch the two unknown wasps quarrel. Once that spectator wasp sees one of them, it will know whether or not it needs to fight for dominance.

According to recent reports, “They will treat the winner of that fight independently in a third interaction differently than they would the loser,” Jernigan explained. “Despite having these small brains and relatively simple vision, they have these really complex social lives that revolve around this specialized ability to recognize each other.”.

According to the team, understanding this facial recognition could help us understand human brain systems as well.

Industry observers note that “This system, hopefully, holds the potential to help us understand our own brains as we study the circuit connections and the role of experience in giving rise to identity recognition,” Jernigan said. “It’s really remarkable that they have this kind of really human-like or primate-like ability that you wouldn’t typically expect for an insect. And I think it’s almost unbelievable that they have some of the similar kind of neural computations for doing a similar task as we do. It takes a tremendous amount of neural connections to do something similar in a primate.”.

  • "This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout. The tires use a sensor that looks a lot like a Dexcom G7 to feed temperature, air pressure, acceleration, and identification data to a vehicle's computers.

Recent findings suggest that that information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data. For example, swap your summer tires for squishier winter rubber, and a compatible car could recognize the change and automatically adjust how its electronic controls intervene, leaving you free to imagine a world where maybe we all just drove better.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94043.

"This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani. The sensor, weighing just 13 grams, is bonded to the tire's inner liner beneath the tread using a specially developed adhesive and rubber housing. The process was developed using learnings from Pirelli's Noise Cancelling System, which uses foam inside the tire to absorb sound waves and reduce cabin vibration. The sensor must survive extreme temperatures, constant flexing, and the insane lateral g-forces that tires are susceptible to at over 200 mph. Engineers explained that its battery is designed to outlast the tire and enters a low-power sleep mode during extended storage.

Sources indicate that the more inspiring part is what the car does with the information it gathers. As we found in our recent all-weather tire comparison test, summer, winter, and all-season tires perform dramatically differently. Yet a vehicle's electronic controls are generally calibrated around its original equipment, using things like wheel speed sensors that aren’t as close to the road surface as the Cyber Tyre. Instead, it identifies the specific tire installed at each corner, allowing it to use different wheel-slip targets. And with the sensor attached to the inside of the tire, the data informing those systems is closer to the road surface than ever.

We sampled the technology at Las Vegas Motor Speedway in two Mercedes-AMG GT63 S four-doors wearing Cyber Tyre-equipped P Zero MS all-season tires.

The first exercise had us pin the throttle through a corner from 40 mph using three different traction-control calibrations, all on the same P Zero MS all-season tires. The first, intended for ultra-high-performance summer tires, was overly restrictive, cutting power before the tires could deliver much acceleration. The second, calibrated for winter tires, permitted considerably more wheelspin, making the AMG easy to slide. Despite that setting being the most fun (and our favorite), Cyber Tyre delivered a happy medium, allowing more controlled acceleration without either extreme.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94043.

This is where Cyber Tyre begins to make the case against selectable drive modes. The same car, wearing the same tires, just behaved three different ways without any mechanical changes. It's not going to replace the button that stiffens your dampers or changes your exhaust note, but it could eventually make some traction-related settings redundant.

The second AMG demonstrated ABS braking from 65 mph. With Cyber Tyre integration active, our stopping distance improved by 0.9 meter, or about three feet, according to Pirelli's instrumentation. That's not dramatically different, but still a measurable improvement.

Industry observers note that of course, these demonstrations weren't proof that Cyber Tyre can outperform a conventional system already calibrated for the correct tires. And the technology isn't smart enough to know it's snowing just because the tires are cold. But the distinction is that Cyber Tyre can give the car information about its tires without the driver doing anything. That could be super useful as tires wear, temperatures change, or owners swap between summer and winter sets. Pirelli is also developing tire-wear estimates using its sensor data, which could prove useful for fleet operators managing hundreds of vehicles.

Pirelli and Bosch announced their development partnership in 2024, and the technology has already appeared in vehicles from McLaren and Pagani. Pirelli executives say a substantially higher-volume application should be announced in the first half of 2027, with production expected in 2028. So it's possible this tech could arrive in models as common as a Ford pickup.

Industry observers note that pirelli is also investing approximately $1.2 billion to expand its Rome, Georgia, manufacturing facility, where Cyber Tyre-equipped products will be produced alongside conventional tires. By 2033, the company expects annual production capacity to reach six million tires and plans to add up to 1000 engineering jobs.

It has been revealed that they also recently revealed that China's state-owned Sinochem, formerly Pirelli's largest shareholder, reduced its ownership to 13.6 percent in November. The Italian government has restricted Sinochem's influence and specifically prohibited sharing Cyber Tyre data with entities connected to the Chinese government. Following those governance changes, Pirelli received U.S. authorization to market the technology here. Not that anyone was worried about a Pagani Utopia Roadster being a boon of classified information.

Cyber Tyre isn't about to take the Ford Bronco's G.O.A.T. modes out back to shoot them. There are plenty of reasons to let drivers decide how their cars behave. But after experiencing three dramatically different calibrations in the same AMG, it's easy to see why some of those decisions might eventually be better left to the car. Just make sure we’re able to fully disable them.

Austin Irwin has worked for Car and Driver for over 10 years in various roles. He's steadily worked his way from an entry-level data entry position into driving vehicles for photography and video, and is now reviewing and testing cars. What will he do next? Who knows, but he better be fast.

World’s fastest soft robot sprints 15 feet per second

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2022, researchers at the University of California San Diego developed a 3D-printed soft robot that used air power to scuttle along at a modest 1.5 inches per second.
  • “Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow.
  • According to recent reports, the invention’s speed comes from a novel compound steam engine that allows highly pressurized air to expand throughout numerous chambers not once but twice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2022, researchers at the University of California San Diego developed a 3D-printed soft robot that used air power to scuttle along at a modest 1.5 inches per second. After a few years of adjustments, the engineering team now has a six-legged iteration that leaves its predecessor in the dust. Detailed in a study published in the journal Science Robotics, their newly introduced soft robot still contains no electronics, but runs across multiple types of terrain at speeds topping 15 feet per second. According to its designers, the machine is the fastest soft robot ever constructed.

“Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow. We hoped to overcome this limitation, and we were fortunate to find a solution to make the new robot 100 times faster,” Yichen Zhai, a study co-author and UC San Diego engineer, noted in a statement.

According to recent reports, the invention’s speed comes from a novel compound steam engine that allows highly pressurized air to expand throughout numerous chambers not once but twice. This air first flows through the robot’s valves, then recirculates through wider, lower-pressure sections in its legs. The team’s creation maintained its efficiency and speed in multiple environments, including gravel, grass, mulch, and concrete. It even handles sandy surfaces and can work underwater.

In a recent development, “The key challenge was to implement a time-tested solution (the compound steam engine) in a soft running robot that can be printed in a single piece out of a single material,” explained Zhai. “We see this as a step towards complex and powerful robots that can be printed on the desktop using inexpensive materials.”.

Their current version of the robot is still limited by its power source, and the tethered hose that delivers the pressurized. That said, they strategy to design future variants requiring less air. This would hypothetically allow them to attach a portable power source like a compressed air cartridge, as well as enable more complex controls and maneuvering.

These prototypes are more than oddball experiments, too. Without any onboard electronics, similar robots could have an advantage while operating in highly irradiated environments, dangerous conditions, and even outer space.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Trump says he “protected” Elon Musk during his first term, and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” He tied it to “a certain incident” that he called “a tough incident,” but he didn’t say what it was.
  • Musk had plenty of run-ins with federal regulators between 2017 and 2021.
  • Industry observers note that trump called in to CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Trump says he “protected” Elon Musk during his first term, and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” He tied it to “a certain incident” that he called “a tough incident,” but he didn’t say what it was.

Musk had plenty of run-ins with federal regulators between 2017 and 2021. One of them could have ended his career as a public company CEO, and it’s our best guess.

Industry observers note that trump called in to CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday. That same morning, Nvidia’s board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, and in its press release it said it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” before concluding Huang posed no national security risk.

Trump argued that the US needs to “protect our geniuses.” Then he brought up Musk:.

Recent findings suggest that “You know, I protected Elon in my first term. Very significant. Elon was protected. I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon. I love Elon. I think he’s great. You know, 80% super genius, 20% he has other problems. But I tell him that. But Elon, I protected. You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me. And, you know, a certain incident took place, which was, you know, a tough incident.”.

Industry observers note that it’s not the first time he has hinted at it. Last week, in a Fox News interview from Shenzhen, Trump mentioned: “I helped Elon a lot in my first term. I helped him a lot. He was in major trouble.” Back in 2024, he told CNBC he had helped Musk “when I was president,” again without details.

Recent findings suggest that on August 7, 2018, Musk tweeted that he was “considering taking Tesla private at $420. Funding secured.” It wasn’t. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had shown interest, but no deal or price had been agreed, and the take-private strategy was dead within three weeks.

Industry observers note that the SEC sued Musk for securities fraud on September 27, 2018. The agency didn’t only ask for a fine. It asked the court to bar Musk from serving as an officer or director of any public tech giant. That would have meant no more Elon at Tesla, which lines up with “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me” better than anything else on this list.

And then it went away fast. Two days later, the SEC announced a settlement: Musk stayed CEO, gave up the chairman title for three years, and he and Tesla each paid $20 million, $40 million in total. Tesla added two independent directors and agreed to have a lawyer pre-approve Musk’s material tweets, but the SEC never fully enforced it. Musk didn’t admit or deny anything.

The SEC was run at the time by Jay Clayton, a Trump appointee.

According to recent reports, there was a criminal side too. In September 2018, federal prosecutors in San Francisco opened a fraud investigation over the same tweet. It never led to charges, and the Justice Department never remarked publicly why.

The SEC came back in February 2019 and asked a judge to hold Musk in contempt after he tweeted Tesla production guidance without pre-approval. That one ended in April with an amended deal listing the topics he needed approval for, and no new penalty.

In May 2020, Musk reopened the Fremont factory in defiance of Alameda County’s COVID orders and tweeted: “If anyone is arrested, I ask that it only be me.” Trump tweeted the next day that California “should let Tesla & @elonmusk open the plant, NOW.” But the county was already working toward a reopening date of May 18, and a president doesn’t control county health orders.

According to recent reports, there’s also the September 2018 Joe Rogan episode, where Musk smoked a joint on camera. NASA followed with a workplace safety review of SpaceX and Boeing, and SpaceX lives on federal contracts.

For context, Musk sat on Trump’s business advisory councils early in that first term, and quit in June 2017 when Trump pulled out of the Paris Agreement. That feels like a lifetime ago now that xAI runs its data centers on natural gas turbines.

Our money is on “funding secured.”.

Musk declared a take-private deal at a specific price that the other side never agreed to, and the stock jumped. It’s textbook securities fraud. The SEC asked to remove him from public company leadership, and two days later he got a $20 million fine, an insignificant amount of money for him, and lost a mostly insignificant title. For someone who’s now worth hundreds of billions, that’s a slap on the wrist.

The main remedy was supposed to be independent oversight. Tesla gave the chair to Robyn Denholm, who had been on the board since 2014, and the board has done what Musk wanted ever since: it defended his pay packages, approved upcoming ones, and stayed quiet while the brand took damage. Denholm herself has sold tens of millions of dollars in TSLA along the way. The SEC got a governance fix on paper and nothing in practice.

It has been revealed that just imagine where Tesla would be if a product oriented CEO had taken over from Elon in early 2018. The tech giant would have spent the last 6 years developing new models instead of betting the farm on autonomy. The Cybertruck almost certainly does not happen, at least not in its current form. Instead, they would have developed a more conventional pickup. We'd have gotten 2nd generation models of the X and S instead of them being canceled. Instead of a Cybercab, there would be a model 2 compact car people could buy. And there would likely be a Tesla van and a full sized SUV, possibly developed on the same underlying platform. Also, the SEC was trying to ban him from running public companies. At the time, SpaceX was still private. So, Elon could have still run SpaceX.

Trump likes to take credit, and he could be inflating his role here. But if the White House leaned on the SEC or the Justice Department in 2018 to help a CEO facing fraud allegations, that’s a serious problem, and someone should look into it.

In a recent development, the timing doesn’t help. He remarked it the same day he appears to have intervened to reinstate Huang as CEO of Nvidia.

So what exactly did the administration do in 2018, and what does Musk owe for it?

#155652. The Porsche 718 Boxster EV Does a Convincing Impression of a Sports Car

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1601 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Roadandtrack ↗ Open Full Page

The Porsche 718 Boxster EV Does a Convincing Impression of a Sports Car

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the most important detail about the electric Porsche 718 Boxster isn’t that it’s an EV, it’s that it’s a Porsche sports car.
  • It has been revealed that I won’t keep you in suspense.
  • In a recent development, where Porsche put the 800-volt battery pack in the Boxster flips the “every EV drives the same” trope on its side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the most important detail about the electric Porsche 718 Boxster isn’t that it’s an EV, it’s that it’s a Porsche sports car. The new electric sports car will be officially unveiled next month, but before then, Porsche is offering up a few details on a black-and-red-camoed platter. More important, beyond the limited intel, I got to spin laps in a prototype at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles. I also rode shotgun while an engineer hotfooted it through the Angeles National Forest.

It has been revealed that I won’t keep you in suspense. As antithetical as an EV might be to the point of a Boxster, this 718 looks, dances, and even sounds (on the inside) like the flat-six-powered machine we’ve known and loved for years. What Porsche put together is an electric car that tries harder than any before at copying the experience of a mid-engine sports car. And there’s a lot more to it than just fake noises.

In a recent development, where Porsche put the 800-volt battery pack in the Boxster flips the “every EV drives the same” trope on its side. Instead of the industry-standard floor-positioned battery pack, the 718 stuffs it exactly where the internal-combustion engine was traditionally housed in the Boxster: right behind the driver’s head. This changes the weight balance from the EV-typical 50/50 to a much more mid-engine-sports-car-like 40/60. The car’s polar moment of inertia is undeniably behind you, a new sensation in the world of electric cars. Maserati planned something similar for the MC20 Folgore but canceled that project before it made production.

Recent findings suggest that other major benefits come with this battery arrangement. Engineers have been able to position the seats just as low in the floor as in the gas-powered Boxster, maintaining a proper sports-car driving position. I can promise nobody will be begging for it to be lower. It helps the design too. While this prototype was covered in camouflage, it was evident that there wasn’t a thick battery pack ruining the Boxster’s proportions. Also unaffected by the transition to electric power are the Boxster trunk and frunk. Just by eyeballing them I could tell that they look to be nearly identical to the previous car in terms of capaciousness.

Deciding how large the battery pack should be was one of the biggest problems Porsche had to solve. We’ll need to wait for the reveal to know the car’s range and battery capacity, but everything is a trade-off when it comes to an electric sports car. All we know about its curb weight is that an “intelligent lightweight construction” will yield a vehicle weight “similar to current 911 models.”.

In a recent development, for reference, a 911 GTS Cabriolet presently comes in around 3700 pounds. After many, many laps around the Porsche Experience Center, my gut tells me the Boxster weighs somewhere in the 3700–4000-pound range. Or, in other words, exceptional for an EV. And not so great compared with the outgoing 718 GTS 4.0, which managed to weigh in under 3200 pounds.

Without range figures to go by, my only reference point for expectations was that the car flashed a “be mindful of range” warning after about 40 minutes of push laps on Porsche’s track. There are plenty of gas-powered sports cars that would be needing a fresh tank at that point too, although obviously not 911s equipped with the extended-range fuel tank.

Recent findings suggest that audible entertainment is handled by Porsche’s E-Shift system, which will come standard. This virtual simulation of a PDK transmission and engine noise debuted in the Taycan, and the latest Boxster is equipped with its own version of the software. Press the button on the steering wheel, and the naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster GTS springs to life over speakers both inside and outside the car.

Engineers painstakingly measured, recorded, and reproduced the sound, then emulated a seven-speed PDK for you to shift through. Unlike the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N or the Genesis GV60 Magma, Porsche does not simulate a gas engine’s torque curve in E-Shift, preferring to maximize performance over experience. That remarked, there are still some theatrics to be found. Downshifting supports “engine” braking via electric-motor regen, and you even hear the “exhaust” popping and crackling on the overrun.

Sources indicate that for many Porsche enthusiasts, it won’t be enough, especially when you remove the roof. The speakers are smart in that Porsche is able to simulate the noise as though it’s coming from behind you in traditional mid-engine fashion. But the spell is easily broken when the wind overpowers the speakers, or you gun it past a wall and there’s no delicious mechanical flat-six howl echoing back at you. It’s fake. I could tell straightaway. And everyone else will too.

According to recent reports, but alas! I had exponentially more fun driving the Boxster with E-Shift than without, especially on the track. You can choose between manual and automatic gearchanges, and I largely left it in automatic. Hearing and remembering where the “engine” revved as I approached the braking zone helped me learn the track rapidly and pick out my braking points by sound alone, very similar to Road & Track’s first experience in the BMW M3 EV prototype running a comparable system.

Then on corner exit, it supplied a faithful throttle reference that helped me trace little slides out of tighter turns in the permissive PSM Sport traction mode. As soon as I turned E-Shift off, I felt lost on the track. And call me old-fashioned, but silently skittering between corners with just the sound of tire squeal is sad. Even more so, because this chassis is a damn good one.

Porsche is being coy with the finer details but let on that numerous chassis components are based on those found in the 911. Boxster owners will be familiar with this hand-me-down strategy, and it continues into the electric era. The steering, braking system, and wheel-and-tire combinations are based on the 911. Pirelli P Zero R summer tires were fitted to staggered wheels (20s in front and 21s in rear) for my time in the car, with a 255-section width in front and a 305-section width in the rear. The new car has PASM damping tech, and engineers note both the damper and spring calibration are softer than those in an equivalent 911. The suspension’s controlled but comfortable composure over rough sections of the road confirmed as much. Thankfully, the brakes just felt like brakes with no weird regen sensation and plenty of feel at the limit.

Sources indicate that my test car didn’t have it, but a sport suspension will also be available. And for the first time, the 718 gets optional rear-axle steering, not to help tighten its turning radius but to supply greater stability at high speeds where the rear wheels can turn in coordination with the fronts. There’s even a front-axle lift, picking up where the Spyder RS left off as the first Boxster with stated feature.

The powertrain itself is all good news. Porsche wouldn’t supply an output number, but the car I drove employs a single electric motor in the rear. It’s reportedly powerful enough for a 0–60-mph run in under three seconds. Porsche says it will be the most powerful 718 so far, meaning more than the 493-hp output of the GT4 RS, and it will almost certainly be the quickest to 60 too. As with Porsche’s other EVs, there’s a push-to-pass mode you can activate for 10 seconds at a time, and using launch control unleashes maximum output too. But at no point was I wanting for more punch around the relatively tight track. Once the tires warmed, launching was effortless, and I didn’t doubt the sub-three-second claim for a moment. The same goes for the road drive, where the Boxster is powerful enough to need serious restraint to not end up doing jail speeds.

In a recent development, porsche Torque Vectoring Plus, another feature derived from the 911, helps dole out power between the two rear wheels to maximum effectiveness. Between this power-distribution system and the Boxster’s happy tendency to kindly bend itself into corners under braking, this 718 has the balance and more jovial nature of the previous one. But another trait carries over: The rear indicates a tendency to dance further out than you would expect from an EV with a more typical 50/50 weight distribution. And despite that Porsche puts big emphasis on keeping weight down (it even reduced the charge ports from its typical two to only one), there was no denying that this Boxster felt porkier than before. The difference was most obvious in the tighter corners where the mass couldn’t be disguised and the grippy front tires ultimately surrendered to the sheer weight that is being asked to turn.

Porsche says it will be launching the electric Boxster into the world with two versions to start. While it wouldn’t reveal the trims, I do know that the version I drove will be the spicier of the two, therefore corresponding with the previous Boxster S. I can’t be certain whether it’s a hit or a miss until I experience the final production car, but I can say this is much more than simply an electric powertrain transplant.

It challenges the hard-core among us in ways EVs simply haven’t before, and if it’s not your cup of tea, don’t worry. Porsche will keep making gas-powered performance cars. It’s just a shame that they won’t start under $100,000, where this one is projected to begin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

Industry observers note that the event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the fresh map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a upcoming progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

In a recent development, developer Embark describes the latest environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the fresh map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The enhancement will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap patch will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

#155650. What We Are Bound To Lose in an Optimized Future

What We Are Bound To Lose in an Optimized Future

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • It has been revealed that december invites a peculiar ritual.
  • This possibility deserves attention as we enter another year of accelerating algorithmic assistance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

It has been revealed that december invites a peculiar ritual. We look back at the year, count our achievements, contemplate our disappointments, and begin constructing a better version of ourselves for January. In 2026, artificial intelligence became an increasingly available accomplice in this exercise. It can summarize our accomplishments, identify inefficiencies, suggest resolutions, and construct an impressively optimized roadmap for 2027. Yet imagine reviewing your year differently. Instead of asking what went according to strategy, consider what happened because it didn't. The conversation you never intended to have. The problem that refused to disappear. The project that demanded more than you thought you could give. Perhaps the moments that changed you most were precisely those that resisted optimization.

This possibility deserves attention as we enter another year of accelerating algorithmic assistance. We have become extraordinarily good at eliminating inconvenience, yet psychological flourishing may depend partly on experiences that cannot be anticipated, accelerated, or outsourced. The interplay between friction and flow offers a way to understand why.

According to recent reports, we generally prefer ease, but our relationship with effort is more complicated than this preference suggests. A 2024 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin confirmed that mental effort is commonly experienced as unpleasant. Yet research published in Cognition in 2025, drawing on six studies involving 2,883 participants, found that exerting effort can increase an activity's perceived meaningfulness. One experiment compared writing with and without ChatGPT assistance. Greater effort contributed to meaning only up to a point. Still, the findings illuminate something that efficiency calculations routinely overlook. We may dislike the difficulty of an experience while valuing what that difficulty allows us to become. This paradox helps explain why flow, the state of intense absorption described by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, cannot simply be manufactured by making everything easier.

A meta-analysis examining the relationship between challenge and skill found that their balance contributes significantly to flow, alongside clear goals and a sense of control. More recent research in Communications Psychology emphasizes autonomy and the personal significance of an activity. Flow emerges through engagement with something sufficiently demanding to absorb us, yet manageable enough to sustain participation. The pianist needs a piece that stretches her abilities; the writer needs an idea that refuses to settle into easy sentences. Friction provides the resistance through which skill becomes experience, and experience becomes satisfaction.

Now consider an algorithmic environment increasingly designed to anticipate our desires and remove obstacles before we encounter them. Recommendations narrow our search; predictive systems streamline our choices, and generative AI can produce results without requiring us to navigate the uncertainties of creation. Such assistance can be enormously beneficial, particularly when it relieves unnecessary burdens. Yet when friction disappears indiscriminately, we risk losing opportunities for the very engagement that makes flow possible. A life engineered for effortless outcomes might become strangely impoverished in the experiences through which we develop competence, confidence, and curiosity. This remains a psychological risk rather than an established destiny, but it raises an essential question: Are we optimizing the quality of our experiences, or merely the speed with which we move through them?

Research suggests that our conventional understanding of a good life may itself be incomplete. Some consider psychological richness a dimension of well-being alongside happiness and meaning. A related 2025 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences describes psychologically rich lives as those containing diverse, interesting, and perspective-changing experiences. To be clear, such experiences are not uniformly pleasant. An unfamiliar place, a challenging encounter, or an unexpected reversal may enlarge our understanding precisely because it disrupts familiar assumptions. This opens an interesting perspective on December's customary stocktaking.

Sources indicate that the experiences that made 2026 psychologically rich may be poorly represented by our conventional measures of success. A friendship deepened through disagreement, an unexpected professional change, or an abandoned proposal that opened an unforeseen possibility might have contributed more to personal development than another efficiently completed task. Of course, hardship is not inherently beneficial. Financial insecurity, discrimination, illness, and exhausting administrative obstacles can diminish well-being and restrict agency. The distinction worth preserving is between friction that erodes our ability to flourish and friction that invites us to exercise it.

Recent findings suggest that the approaching new year makes this distinction painfully relevant. Research on the fresh start effect demonstrates that temporal landmarks, including the beginning of a new year, can motivate humans to pursue aspirations. Perhaps we could use this psychological opening differently in December 2026? Rather than designing another year around the elimination of effort, we might ask which forms of friction deserve a place in our lives. Which difficulties strengthen our abilities? Which uncertainties invite discovery? Which activities would lose their meaning if someone—or something—completed them for us?

The challenge is to choose meaningful friction deliberately, without turning everyday life into an obstacle course. BLISS offers five practical ways to cultivate that judgment.

In a recent development, B — Begin before borrowing. Give your own imagination an opportunity to work before requesting an algorithmic solution.

It has been revealed that L — Let learning take time. Preserve activities in which gradual improvement brings satisfaction, even when shortcuts are readily available.

Industry observers note that I — Invite the unfamiliar. Explore beyond personalized recommendations; seek perspectives and experiences that might challenge established preferences.

In a recent development, S — Stay with the struggle. When a difficulty is productive, resist the urge to eliminate it immediately. Allow yourself the satisfaction of finding a way through.

Sources indicate that S — Save space for surprise. Leave some time unplanned, some questions unanswered, and some possibilities unexplored until they present themselves.

Sources indicate that we can welcome intelligent technologies that reduce unnecessary suffering while protecting the experiences that develop natural intelligence. An increasingly capable algorithmic future need not become a frictionless one, provided we retain the freedom and capacity to choose where human effort matters. As 2026 ends, perhaps the most meaningful resolution for 2027 is not to become more efficient, organized, or productive. It is to become more attentive to what makes life worth living. The winding path through unfamiliar territory may take longer, demand more, and occasionally lead somewhere unexpected. Yet it may also reveal capacities and possibilities that a perfectly optimized route would never allow us to discover.

Sources indicate that we need friction to find flow. And sometimes, the detour is the destination.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, more than 85 years have passed since the very first B-25 bombers rolled off the assembly line. The legendary, twin-engine aircraft flew above every theater of World War II, and were instrumental to the Allied forces’ victory. Many B-25 bombers are preserved in museums, but a handful of them actually remain flightworthy today.

One of those flight-ready B25s is a plane nicknamed Show Me. The aircraft belongs to the Missouri Wing of the Commemorative Air Force, and has taken to the sky every fall since 2009 to demonstrate its impressive aerial bombardment capabilities. But Show Me doesn’t unleash an arsenal of destruction anymore. Instead, the B25 releases a bevy of hollowed-out pumpkins filled with red, white, and blue pool chalk. However, aircraft recently dropped more than gourds for onlookers outside St. Louis. During this year’s flight, Show Me also deployed a pumpkin stuffed with the ashes of the Missouri Wing’s late, beloved volunteer, Lou Tacchi, Jr.

“His family was all on board with it,” current wing commander and retired pilot Rob Jenner told St. Louis public radio. “They had shirts printed up, and they called it the ‘Pop Drop.’”.

Some of Tacchi, Jr.’s ashes were also packed away inside four .50-caliber shells that will now remain aboard the B-25. According to Jenner, their departed colleague will “fly with us forever,” thanks to his final request.

According to recent reports, “[He] had such a deep interest in history, as well as the airplanes, and it was so much a part of his life,” Jenner added. “I think it was natural for him to pick that way to say goodbye.”.

Recent findings suggest that before it received its nickname, Show Me, the B-25 was simply classified by the United States Air Force as 44-31385. It first took to the sky in January 1945 and was used as a trainer for upcoming pilots. Show me is technically a B-25J—the final variant of the aircraft which also featured an eight-gun strafer nose.

Industry observers note that the military retired 44-31385 at Arizona’s Davis Monthan Air Force Base in 1958, before selling it to its first private owner the following year. A windstorm damaged the bomber a decade later while it was stored in Seymour, Illinois. Show Me remained grounded in Seymour until it was finally repaired in 1975. The Commemorative Air Force’s Missouri Wing received the B-25 in 1982.

It has been revealed that the first fully electric Porsche Boxster is finally in the home stretch of development. Ahead of its official debut in early 2027, Porsche offered an early look at the two-door electric sports car.

Despite rumors that the all-electric 718 Boxster was canceled, Porsche confirmed on Tuesday that the Boxster EV will debut in the first quarter of 2027.

“Starting next year, the all-electric 718 Boxster will offer our customers a compelling entry point into the world of two-door sports cars,” Porsche CEO Dr Michael Leiters said.

Ahead of its upcoming debut, Porsche is putting the electric sports car through the paces to ensure it preserves the DNA of its predecessors, a top priority.

Porsche developed a newly introduced “E-Core” architecture specifically for the 718 Boxster to lower the seat position and optimize weight distribution.

With the 800-volt battery mounted directly behind the seats, where the internal combustion engine would typically be found, the weight is concentrated toward the middle of the vehicle. The electric Boxster has a weight distribution of 40% on the front axle and 60% on the rear, matching that of a traditional mid-engined sports car.

It also features an “intelligent lightweight construction,” as Porsche calls it, so the vehicle’s overall weight matches that of the current 911 Cabriolet models with its T-Hybrid powertrain.

“Our engineers have succeeded in transferring the Boxster’s unique concept to the electric world, further enhancing it in the process,” Porsche’s CEO remarked.

The electric Boxster shares many chassis components with the 911, including the steering, which is based on the 911 Carrera GTS. It will offer rear-axle steering, a first for the 718 Boxster.

Meanwhile, the wheel and tire dimensions and braking system are based on the Porsche 911, and the electronically controlled PTV+ limited-slip differential is also pulled from the 911.

Porsche remarked the electric Boxster will be “the most powerful 718 ever,” but didn’t offer a specific output figure.

It has been revealed that tesla is rolling out the 15th iteration of its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, and the update comes with some pretty impressive graphics. It’s called Tesla Reality View, and it’s exactly that, using the vehicle’s cameras to record what’s going on around you, then re-create the scene on the central screen accurately.

Industry observers note that the intent is to show a visual representation of what the latest FSD driver assistance is going to do, as represented by onscreen arrows. Turns are represented, and the screen shows what parking spot the vehicle has selected when using auto park.

Tesla notes the actual driving assistance has also been greatly improved, with an increased ability to spot and react to potholes, small animals, and road debris. The system also uses fleet learning from the trips other Teslas take on the same route, something Tesla has been doing for several iterations of FSD.

How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight.
  • That’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s.
  • “[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight. But for those with eczema, this time of year can wreak havoc on their skin, too.

That’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s. During the winter months, she often dreads the cold.

“[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.

Cold weather and indoor heating can reduce humidity, drying out the skin and triggering or worsening eczema flare-ups.

“[What we know] about the skin barrier is that it really is like a gate or wall against the outside world,” Camille Howard-Verovic, MD, a dermatologist at Active Dermatology, told Healthline.

According to recent reports, in healthy skin, the barrier controls what enters and leaves the skin. However, for people with eczema, Howard-Verovic noted they have skin barrier dysfunction, which allows substances such as allergens and irritants to penetrate the skin.

Cold weather can increase transepidermal water loss, a process in which moisture escapes through the skin’s outer barrier and evaporates into the surrounding air.

According to recent reports, “People with eczema have a tremendous amount of transepidermal water loss, so you’re just drier,” said Howard-Verovic. “[You’re] not holding onto the water as well, so that causes the itching and the rash that we feel when we have eczema.”.

Rowland first noticed eczema flares behind her ears as well as on her elbows, arms, and the back of her knees.

“[It] looked like a rash, so that’s what I thought it was all this time, and I dealt with it for so long until after I had my son and then it started to get worse on my face,” she noted.

She eventually went to a dermatologist who diagnosed her with moderate-to-severe eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that can cause intense itching, painful skin cracking, thickened skin, and redness or swelling.

When Rowland learned that eczema can be genetic, it made sense to her.

“I remember seeing substantial rashes on [my mom’s] neck and her arms…so she had it, and I guess I was the lucky one,” said Rowland.

At first, she tried eliminating foods that she thought might be triggers. She also bathed in oatmeal.

In a recent development, “[I] literally have had a tub full of oatmeal, like literally went to the store to get store-bought fresh oats,” she mentioned. “I tried everything, and it doesn’t help until you go talk to a doctor about it.”.

At first, she tried prescription topical medications but found them cumbersome.

“I don’t have the time, if I’m being honest, and we live in a world that is moving so fast…I started buying like three tubes of whatever it was I was using and losing it; it was just too much for me,” Rowland remarked.

Rowland said she found relief with Ebglyss, a prescription injectable medication for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. She has also partnered with Eli Lilly and Tech giant, its manufacturer, to raise awareness about eczema.

Rowland noted she’s sharing her experience to help others living with eczema, including people she’s met who have experienced greater challenges managing the condition.

“One lady was telling me about how she’s having a tough time [looking] in the mirror cause she doesn’t know who’s looking back at her, and she saw her skin before eczema and after,” mentioned Rowland.

When she first had symptoms, she noted she felt embarrassed, too.

“[Because] it was just in the middle of my arm space and…[if I] put out my hand to shake someone’s hand, you don’t know if somebody’s judgy,” she noted.

Rowland hopes being open about her condition will encourage others to advocate for themselves and talk with their doctor about treatment options.

Because eczema can look different on deeper skin tones, Howard-Verovic noted that a dermatologist can help make the correct diagnosis.

It has been revealed that “Some people may not even know that they have eczema,” she remarked. “We know that eczema is a rash; it can appear red on certain skin tones, and it can be grey or white on certain skin tones, so it can look a little different.”.

In addition to medication, Rowland said managing stress helps reduce her eczema flare-ups.

“Before [when] I went on tour, because I was under so much stress, it flared up like crazy, like you wouldn’t believe,” she said. “We were in the back trying to figure out how to cover certain things up, and we figured some of it out, and some of it was really tricky, but what helped was when I actually just calmed down…not that it helped overnight, but it did just kind of bring the flare down.”.

She noted red light therapy, feeling grounded outside without her shoes on, getting vitamin D from natural sunlight, and cooking are ways she reduces ongoing stress.

In a recent development, “Cooking calms me when my kids aren’t here, and I have a really good [Zen] playlist on,” said Rowland. “[If] you ask me a question [in those moments], I might give you my heart; I’m just so happy.”.

She also tries to cut back on sugar, which she believes triggers flares.

Another way to reduce flares, according to Howard-Verovic, is to avoid hot showers, especially in the winter.

“[We] know eczematous skin likes lukewarm water,” she said.

Because Howard-Verovic and her daughter both live with eczema, she set a rule about when it’s time to get out of the shower.

“[If] you see condensation on the bathroom mirror, you’ve spent too much time in the shower,” said Howard-Verovic. “[That] really hot, hot water feels really good in that moment…but when you get out all that water evaporates, and there’s no moisture in the atmosphere, and it dries your skin out, and now your skin is unhappy again.”.

If you prefer to take baths, she mentioned use gentle cleansers.

“[There] are bleach baths for really, really bad flare-ups,” she noted.

Diluted bleach baths are sometimes recommended for people with eczema, but they should only be used according to a healthcare professional’s instructions.

As soon as you get out of the shower or bath, Howard-Verovic said to apply a quality moisturizer to your damp skin. According to the National Eczema Association (NEA), lotions containing the following ingredients can help ease dry skin associated with eczema.

To help identify appropriate products, look for ones that have the NEA’s Seal of Acceptance.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A jingle-playing, googly-eyed team of trash-collecting robots are vying to make the world’s busiest rail station a bit cleaner.
  • East Japan Railway Company (referred to as JR East), which runs several lines in Tokyo’s bustling Shinjuku Station, recently wrapped up a roughly 10-week trial of these eye-catching robots.
  • Recent findings suggest that each of the three robots sports a different color (green, yellow, or red) to match their accompanying rail line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A jingle-playing, googly-eyed team of trash-collecting robots are vying to make the world’s busiest rail station a bit cleaner.

East Japan Railway Company (referred to as JR East), which runs several lines in Tokyo’s bustling Shinjuku Station, recently wrapped up a roughly 10-week trial of these eye-catching robots. The machines stand just over three feet tall, and roll autonomously along preprogrammed routes through the station’s underground concourses between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. Once full, they trundle back to the station’s garbage collection area on their own.

Recent findings suggest that each of the three robots sports a different color (green, yellow, or red) to match their accompanying rail line. They definitely don’t look like your average sad, overflowing waste bin. Instead, they stroll up to commuters with bright lights and a front-facing screen showing cartoon eyes. Music appears to play when trash gets fed into them. An accompanying illustration of  Shinjukuma, the station’s bear mascot, shows passengers which bins are for general trash and which are for plastic bottles. It’s all very Japanese.

JR East officials are hoping these bins on wheels will help relieve some of the burden on garbage collectors who struggle to keep up with trash generated by the millions  of people  passing through every day. The station, which sits on the western edge of central Tokyo, sees nearly three million daily passengers, an absurd amount of foot traffic that earned it a Guinness World Record. But more people means more trash. According to Tokyo Weekender, sanitation workers in the station unload garbage from fixed bags more than 10 times per day.

It has been revealed that the robots could help, but only if they don’t get in the way and create more problems than they solve. Though JR East reportedly tested out a pair of garbage robots back in 2023, that was in a much smaller station and only for three days. Shinjuku is a much bigger challenge and serves as a kind of stress test to see if they are able to operate safely and effectively in densely packed areas.

Tokyo isn’t the only city experimenting with trash robots. A cat-themed, mobile trash unit made a brief appearance in Paris’ Charles De Gaulle airport last year. In Singapore, an autonomous robot started collecting garbage in 2019 at Jewel Changi Airport, the shopping complex attached to the city’s main airport. And while trash collection is still relatively niche, automated cleaning robots are quickly becoming mainstays in many modern transportation hubs. Houston, Baltimore, Pittsburgh, and Oakland are among the many  cities in the United States already putting robot cleaners to work scrubbing and mopping airport floors.

Making these robots seem cute isn’t just for attracting selfies. It’s also a self-defense strategy. Humans have a mixed track record when it comes to sharing space with robots. In 2024, the Newly introduced York Police Department retired a 400-pound, egg-shaped surveillance robot from patrolling subway lines after facing pushback from privacy activists and concerned citizens, some of whom felt uncomfortable near the lifeless, imposing monitor. Years earlier, a friendly hitchhiking robot called HitchBot made it about two weeks into its trip across the United States when it was found vandalized and beheaded in Philadelphia.

Could cartoon eyes and a cute mascot have saved those robots? It’s difficult to say, but at least the Tokyo garbage robots seemed to make it through their trial without any dissected parts. That’s an improvement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that back in 2016, Land Rover ended production of the old-school Defender. Ineos CEO Jim Ratcliffe then entered the automotive market to fill the niche with the defiantly old-school Grenadier SUV and its pickup truck counterpart, the Quartermaster. Ineos describes the vehicles as offering “rugged British spirit and design with German engineering rigor.” And soon, the brand will add “American-made” to that mix.

On Tuesday, Ineos Automotive confirmed it is moving Grenadier and Quartermaster production to the United States. The move will happen in 2028, with production moving to an undetermined location in America; an announcement on that should come within a few months. As part of the shuffle, Ineos Automotive notes it will sell its current plant in Hambach, France to Chinese automaker BYD, but the brand will still build Grenadier and Quartermaster vehicles in Hambach while it sets up American facilities.

Sources indicate that “Americans have already taken the Grenadier to their hearts, and U.S. policies that have created an incredibly attractive, pro-growth business environment. Setting up production there makes so much sense. It will empower us to invest, expand, and reach even more customers around the world,” Ineos Automotive CEO Lynn Calder mentioned in a statement.

This move should make a lot of sense for Ineos. 70 percent of the brand’s global sales are in the U.S. market, so moving production stateside would leave the brand far less exposed to American import tariffs. The Trump administration has imposed a 15 percent tariff on European Union-built vehicles, and the Quartermaster is subject to the 25 percent “chicken tax,” which dates back to the 1960s and protects the U.S. pickup truck market. Alleviating the tariff burden would allow Ineos Automotive to lower prices further, improve profit margins—or, potentially, both.

Ineos Automotive’s announcement made no mention of the purportedly still-upcoming Fusilier, expected to launch as an EV and range-extended EV later this decade. Initial intends called for Austrian manufacturer Magna, maker of the Mercedes G-Class, to engineer and build the Fusilier at its plant in Austria.

#155643. What Darwin’s Bees Tell Us About Right and Wrong

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)

What Darwin’s Bees Tell Us About Right and Wrong

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • Evolutionary explanations of morality have been of scientific interest since at least Darwin.
  • This is why I’ve recently published an academic article on the topic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

Evolutionary explanations of morality have been of scientific interest since at least Darwin. Proto-Darwinian explanations, however, have been around for much longer. The attempt to explain morality has a long tradition going back as far as ancient Greece.

This is why I’ve recently published an academic article on the topic.

Protagoras, in one of Plato’s dialogues, provides perhaps the first scientific explanation of morality as a set of norms and enforcement agencies, an invention of humanity to escape a Hobbesian state of nature. Couched in terms of a myth, we may treat this as a mere just-so story.

Recent findings suggest that much later, David Hume came astonishingly close to providing a Darwinian explanation of morality himself. Rainer Hegselmann and Oliver Will identify four key components of Hume’s account: a pre-societal human nature with confined generosity, the invention of artificial values to be reinforced and internalized through the approval and disapproval of others, a division of labor reaping the benefits of cooperation and trust, and the invention of central authorities that monitor, enforce, and eventually punish behavior.

These accounts, a mere story and myth in the case of Protagoras and an informal suggestion of a how-possibly explanation in the case of Hume, leave much to be desired, but they were nevertheless the best explanations available at the time.

Recent findings suggest that luckily, it did not take two millennia for the next advancement. Less than a century after Hume’s death, Darwin delivered the means for pushing the inquiry into human morality further, filling a gap Hume could only describe as nature.

In a recent development, darwin himself suggested that the origin of morality can be explained with his theory. He did not maintain that any social animal, if its intellectual faculties were to become as highly developed as ours, would acquire exactly the same moral sense. If, to take his extreme case, humans were reared under precisely the same conditions as hive-bees, our unmarried females would, like the worker-bees, “think it a sacred duty to kill their brothers.” Mothers would strive to kill their fertile daughters, and no one would think of interfering. Nevertheless, the bee, or any other social animal, would gain, as it appeared to Darwin, some feeling of right or wrong, or a conscience.

Industry observers note that the thought is unsettling. What a creature feels to be right and wrong depends on the kind of creature it is and the conditions under which it lives.

This, of course, is still “just” a how-possibly explanation, or, as critics like to call them, a just-so story. It should be clear, however, that from Protagoras over to Hume to Darwin, significant improvements in the explanation of morality have been made, with more and more gaps being closed. Explanations come in degrees, and this research program is providing better and better explanations.

Unfortunately, it took a while until informal evolutionary explanations resting on the good of the species were replaced with formal models from evolutionary game theory, showing that the origin of moral behavior is not much of a mystery after all. The philosopher Brian Skyrms was the first to apply evolutionary game theory to unpack Hume’s account in a formal manner, with others following in the creation of upcoming models and simulations.

These sets of models strengthen our confidence that morality could have evolved in a way envisioned by Hume and Darwin, providing considerable explanatory power, even though empirical work has, hitherto, been largely left out of the picture.

Modelers such as Skyrms simply continue an old philosophical school of thought with the modern tools of science, a move that ought to be encouraged. Even the work of moral philosophers in this Humean tradition has been very empirical and guided by science, trying to unpack the idea of morality being a mere artifact. It is a case in point for the division of labor between philosophers, modelers, and empirical researchers.

Akin to other primates, evolution equipped us with emotions and other cognitive machinery in order to solve interdependent decision problems. We do not know yet which of our moral attitudes are hard-wired and which are culturally acquired, but that is obviously no reason not to ask the question. Darwin’s bees tell us what kind of answer to expect: one that depends on the problems of living together that a species has to solve.

On the Precipice of the Abyss has tendrils in many areas of the game, touching several parts of its fiction as well as gameplay, so it’s one to watch out for.

Version 2.4’s biggest claim to fame is the introduction of the Krampus Compliance Authority, a fresh faction that’s affiliated with TOPS. This looks to be the oversight committee, dispatched after the squad’s adventure beneath Timesworn Hill.

Dialyn relies on two resources: Customer Complaint and Positive Review, but her core role is to stun enemies and allow teammates to unleash their Ults, with a nice boost to boot.

Banyue is another S-Rank, though he’s a Fire Rupture Agent. He uses his martial arts expertise to create combinations of might and grandeur. In combat, he pulls from Adrenaline and Wrathful Fires, alternating between the two to fuel his actions. There’s a bit of rhythm to his gameplay that might take you a little while to master.

Even more characters will join as part of this revision, in the form of not one but two new Bangboo units. Birkblick is Krampus' own proprietary lil bunny fella, who brings a sensor array that can transform into a cannon in combat, essentially tracking and immediately nuking targets. Then there’s Bild N. Boolok, a Support Agent-affiliated Physical damage dealing Bangboo bringing a giant block hammer to the fight to, well, smash enemies with.

It’s a bit of a winter party in Version 2.4, it seems, as the update will bring back Hugo (Attack - Ice), and Ellen (Attack - Ice), too.

In a recent development, you can also look forward to the return of the Bangboo auto chess event, which now includes PvE stages with unique rewards. In fact, playing this event is how you could get Bild N. Boolok for free. Lightstream Notes is another event that will be available for the duration of this update, and it will let you tag along with Ye Shunguang to New Eridu.
